```{r setup}
show_fig <- function(path, caption, alt, id, width = NULL) {
  # `caption` is the full, visible figure caption (becomes the figure's
  # caption text via pandoc's implicit-figure handling). `alt` is a
  # short, separate description for screen readers, passed through via
  # pandoc's image `{alt="..."}` attribute, per UNR's own accessibility
  # guidance, alt text should be succinct (roughly under 150 characters),
  # while the full descriptive caption stays as real, visible text.
  # `id` sets the figure's Quarto crossref id (e.g. "fig-timeline"), so
  # it renders as a numbered "Figure N" and can be cited by number via
  # @id in the prose. `width` (e.g. "55%") constrains the rendered
  # width -- needed for a handful of naturally very tall (portrait)
  # source images, which otherwise scale to the full text width and
  # overflow past the bottom margin in the PDF/LaTeX output (confirmed
  # directly: an unconstrained tall image pushed its own caption text
  # into the page-number footer).
  abs_path <- file.path(normalizePath(getwd()), path)
  abs_path <- gsub("\\\\", "/", abs_path)
  alt_escaped <- gsub('"', "'", alt)
  width_attr <- if (is.null(width)) "" else sprintf(' width="%s"', width)
  knitr::asis_output(sprintf('![%s](%s){#%s fig-alt="%s"%s}', caption, abs_path, id, alt_escaped, width_attr))
}
```

# Introduction

## Study area and setting

Steamboat Hills sits a few kilometers south of Reno, Nevada, at the
northern end of a fault-bounded belt of Great Basin geothermal systems.
Unlike most Great Basin systems, which are amagmatic and derive their heat
from regionally elevated mantle heat flow alone, Steamboat is one of a
small number of magmatic-influenced systems in the province, and it is one
of the longest-studied hydrothermal areas in the western United States,
characterized geologically and hydrologically since the 1950s
[@thompsonwhite1964; @white1964b; @white1968c; @silberman1979]. The field
has produced electricity commercially since the mid-1980s and is currently
operated by Ormat Technologies as a binary, fully reinjected system
generating on the order of 79 MW net [@dhakal2025]. Production and
injection are conventionally divided into three thermal zones (Upper,
Middle, and Lower Steamboat) reflecting a natural-state upflow of roughly
220-240 degrees Celsius beneath Upper Steamboat that cools northeastward
along strike toward the Middle and Lower fields [@dhakal2025;
@johnsonhulen2006].

At the surface, this deep system expresses itself through the Lower Sinter
Terrace, an area of active and historically active fumaroles, seeps, and
hot springs within the Steamboat Springs Area of Critical Environmental
Concern. That surface expression has not been static. Sorey and Colvard
[@sorey1992] documented a near-total cessation of natural spring flow at
the main and low silica terraces between 1986 and 1989, attributing most
(though not all) of the decline to regional shallow-groundwater drawdown
rather than to geothermal production. Sorey [@sorey2000] revisited the same
terrace roughly a decade later and found that although regional groundwater
levels had by then recovered, natural spring flow at the main terrace had
not resumed. That non-recovery is the single most important piece of
historical context for this proposal: it establishes that surface discharge
at Steamboat is not simply a mirror of groundwater level, and that a system
which goes quiet does not necessarily reawaken on its own.

It was against that backdrop that, beginning around 2022, steaming ground
at the Lower Sinter Terrace began to expand again, and on June 3, 2025, an
uncapped, shallow abandoned well erupted without warning, sending boiling
water roughly 30 meters into the air: the first geyser-like activity
documented at Steamboat in decades [@lindsey2026]. The well was capped in
the following days to weeks, but discharge did not stop; it redistributed
laterally, opening new seeps and spitting vents along nearby fractures.
This event, and the still-open question of what it means for the system's
deeper plumbing, motivates this proposal: a direct re-examination of
Sorey's own chloride-discharge method against the modern system, and a test
of whether continuous conductivity monitoring can substitute for discrete
chloride sampling as a practical way to track that outflow going forward.

## A brief chronology

Three broad periods structure this history, shown in @fig-timeline. The
**historical/characterization period** (roughly 1950-1968) established
the regional geology, structure, and hydrology that every later study,
including this one, still relies on [@thompsonwhite1964; @white1964b;
@white1968c]. The **development period** (1986-2007) covers the
transition from a natural system to a commercially produced one, the
1987-89 spring-flow decline documented by Sorey and Colvard
[@sorey1992], its non-recovery by 2000 [@sorey2000], and the buildout
of the groundwater/geothermal monitor-well network described by
Klein, Johnson, and Spielman [@klein2007]. The **reawakening period**
(2022-present) covers the renewed steaming, the June 2025 eruption,
and this project's own response.

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 1860-1862 | Earliest published record of geyser observations in the United States, at Steamboat [@white1968c]. |
| 1950 | USGS thermal-gradient and chemistry test holes drilled [@white1968c]. |
| 1964 | Regional geology and structure of the Steamboat Springs area described [@thompsonwhite1964; @white1964b]. |
| 1968 | Hydrology, activity, and heat flow of the thermal system characterized in detail [@white1968c]. |
| 1986 | Commercial production begins. |
| 1987-1989 | Natural hot-spring flow at the main and low silica terraces declines and ceases [@sorey1992]. |
| 1992 | Sorey and Colvard attribute most of the spring-flow decline to regional groundwater drawdown, not geothermal production [@sorey1992]. |
| 2000 | Groundwater levels recover, but natural spring flow does not resume at the main terrace [@sorey2000]. |
| 2007 | The groundwater/geothermal monitor-well network is documented in detail [@klein2007]. |
| 2022 | Water begins accumulating in the fissure's "Big Pool" and steaming ground expands at the Lower Sinter Terrace, the first signs of renewed activity (the Busick property fissure and pipe had reportedly been dry for years before this) [@lindsey2026; NBMG field timeline, 2024]. |
| 2023 | The fissure fills with water and sustained bubbling begins by November; a new fumarole forms near the Hot Springs Resort parking lot. Diffuse steaming measurably expands across the terrace, though no focused vents or flowing water are seen yet [@lindsey2026; NBMG field timeline, 2024]. |
| 2024-03 | A site visit documents sustained bubbling in the fissure, a boiling "Driveway Spring," and a new fumarole with fresh sulfur staining; activity shifts from diffuse degassing to localized seeps and vents over the year [@lindsey2026; NBMG field timeline, 2024]. |
| 2025 (May) | Sustained bubbling and spouting resume in the fissure 1-2 weeks before the eruption; existing vents intensify and discharge points migrate along nearby fractures [@lindsey2026; NBMG field timeline, 2024]. |
| 2025-05-30 | Ormat's field-wide authorized injection limit is raised from 49,500 to 55,000 gpm (NDEP UIC Temporary Permit UNEV2007204T2025-1 [@nevadadep2025uic]), about two weeks before the eruption; a candidate contributing factor, not yet confirmed (see below). |
| 2025-06-01/02 | A geyser erupts overnight from the Busick property pipe, reported at an estimated 100 ft before moderating to 20-30 ft by morning and ceasing by afternoon; a resident report brings NBMG to the site within hours (NBMG field timeline, 2024). |
| 2025-06-05/06 | A second eruption pulse begins overnight and is surveyed in detail the next morning: drone-estimated bursts of 8-12 m (to 18 m), the "Driveway Spring" measured at 95.1 C, new fumaroles to 95.8 C, and a previously unsurveyed warm spring at 40.0 C (NBMG field timeline, 2024). |
| 2025 | The wellhead is capped and discharge redistributes laterally [@lindsey2026]. NBMG begins an integrated monitoring program. |
| 2026 | The eruption is formally documented [@lindsey2026]; this project deploys temperature loggers (April) and stream conductivity loggers (July 15); spring and well remapping and renewed chemistry sampling continue under this thesis. In August, the author and Dave find a new seep-fed hot spring at the terrace (GPS-logged and photographed the following month, September 27); a growing sulfur deposit and new alluvium-to-sinter seeps are documented the same month. |

## Candidate explanations for the reactivation

What actually drove the 2022-2025 reactivation is an open question this
proposal does not claim to resolve, but several candidate explanations
already have real, if uneven, supporting evidence on file, and are
worth stating together rather than leaving the single injection-permit
event on @fig-timeline unexplained.

**Increased injection pressure/rate (Ormat), with facility context.** The
one dated regulatory document on file (NDEP UIC Temporary Permit
UNEV2007204T2025-1 [@nevadadep2025uic]) raised the field's combined
authorized injection-rate limit from 49,500 to 55,000 gpm on May 30,
2025, about two weeks before the first eruption pulse. The timing is
suggestive, and this is flagged on @fig-timeline as a candidate
contributing factor. It is not confirmed. The permit records newly
*authorized* limits, not the rate actually injected, and the same
document's reported current pressures sit below the prior allowable
ceiling at most wells, so whether injection pressure or rate rose
*before* the eruption, rather than only becoming newly permitted, cannot
be resolved from this one document. @fig-injpressure shows its
well-by-well snapshot: most injection wells were already running close
to their own pressure-limited physical maximum at full production
(77-90 percent of `max_flow_at_allowable_pressure` at IW-5, IW-6, and
42A-32, for example), so the headroom any single well had to inject
more was already limited, whatever the field-wide authorized total
said. That cuts against a reading in which the permit allowed a sudden,
large increase in what was physically happening, without ruling out a
smaller increase at the margin. One well, 23-33, is reported at a
current pressure (135 psig) above its own newly authorized limit (120
psig), which the permit table states as given.

A documented precedent shows why the location of injection, and not only its
total rate, matters for the terraces. Collar [@collar1990thesis] recorded
water-level responses in the alluvial Herz 2 and Brown School wells that
coincided with injection into OESI well IW-3 (completed in tuff breccia),
compared the spring 6 hydrograph directly against the IW-3 injection rate,
and concluded that the reservoir is heterogeneous, with production wells
better connected to the terrace springs than injection wells. His mitigation
proposals (injecting closer to the terrace, perforating the 950-ft zone in
Cox I-1) were aimed at raising head beneath the terraces above land surface,
which is what spring flow requires. The sign was opposite in 1986-89, when
net production lowered heads; for 2025 the question is whether injection
changes raised them, and the June 2025 pipe eruption implies heads at that
spot stood above land surface. This is a mechanism and a precedent, not
evidence that injection caused the 2025 eruption.

The injection question sits inside a longer history of change at the
facility, which the data on file document only partly. Ormat operates
Steamboat as a binary, fully reinjected system [@dhakal2025], and the
Nevada Division of Minerals permit record for Ormat's Steamboat wells
(49 wells, ingested into this project's database) shows continuing
drilling and well-status change across the field rather than a static
configuration: injection well 21-32 was completed in 2014, 42A-32 in
2018, and production well 41-5 in 2012 (now recorded Shut-In); eight of
the 49 permitted wells are recorded Shut-In (seven production, one
injection). A new production well, 28A-32, was spudded July 4, 2026 and
completed August 6, 2026, on the upper hillside near the Shut-In 28-32.
Because 28A-32 post-dates the June 2025 eruption by more than a year,
it cannot have contributed to it; it matters here only as evidence that
field development is ongoing and that the production-injection balance
a future analysis would need to reconstruct is not fixed. Whether
production is declining at the older wells and being replaced elsewhere
on the hill is a reasonable operational question, but the data on file
do not show it: the only repeat production readings available are two
NDEP tracer-test reports (July 2025 and April 2026), in which the one
production well reported, 24-5, fell from 883 to 835 kph (about 5
percent) over nine months, a single well over a short window. Testing
this hypothesis properly needs dated, well-by-well injection and
production histories spanning 2022-2025, which this project has requested
from NDEP (and plans to request them from Ormat; see `docs/action_items_for_user.md`) and does not yet
have.

**Conduit reactivation within the existing hydrothermal system, not a
new fluid source.** This project's own 2026 poster [@irvinlindsey2026]
found that the reactivated fissure's major-ion chemistry and stable
isotopes match the hydrothermal fluid already expressed in nearby
springs and wells, and that paired temperature loggers at the terrace
show a real inverse correlation (r = -0.68) consistent with discharge
redistributing between vents within one connected flow system. The
Cl/B ratio's near-constancy across seven decades (preliminary results,
below) is further, independent support for the same conclusion. Of the
explanations considered here, this one currently has the most direct
observational support.

**Regional groundwater-level recovery remobilizing existing pathways.**
Sorey [-@sorey2000] found that groundwater levels had recovered by 2000
without natural spring flow resuming, which argues that recovery alone
has historically been insufficient to reactivate this system. Whether
a slower, multi-decade continuation of that same recovery eventually
crossed some threshold by 2022 is untested with the data on hand.

**Local seismic triggering.** White [@white1968c] saw definite spring
responses to six of fifteen earthquakes between 1947 and 1952, all moderate
(above about M5) and near, including a 1947 episode in which low-terrace
discharge shifted from spring 25 to spring 50; Collar [@collar1990thesis]
found no link to the largest event of 1986-89 (M3.9, about 11 miles north).
This project's first check used only the three nearest 2025 events (M1.5-1.6),
which are far below any historical response threshold, and found no step in
STMGID water levels. A broader USGS catalog pull (M2.5 and above within 60
km, 2021-2026) finds a more relevant cluster: four M3.0-3.5 events within
about 6 km of the field between 2024-01-29 and 2024-03-09, in the window when
Lindsey and others [@lindsey2026] describe the shift from diffuse steaming to
discrete seeps and vents. Daily water levels at STMGID MW10 (and MW3 from
February 2024) show no consistent step at those events: standardized steps
range from -2.3 to +1.6 across seven comparisons, and none is robust to the
number of tests. That is consistent with the historical pattern that small
events have no detectable effect, but two regional wells outside the field
cannot exclude a local response, so the 2024 cluster is a lead rather than an
explanation. The largest recent regional events (M4.7-4.8 on 19 and 22 April
2026) were about 58 km away. Current support for this explanation is weak.

**Precipitation/recharge-driven.** A large December 2025 storm produced a
modest water-level response at one regional monitoring well but not at a
second, nearby well with a different completion depth, and no precipitation
record exists on file for most of the 2022-2025 reactivation window. Collar
[@collar1990thesis] showed how this question should be tested: 1946-52 spring
discharge tracked annual precipitation, the 1949 drought minimum (48 gpm) was
far above the 1988 flow (3-4 gpm), and a cumulative departure from mean
precipitation at Reno and Sky Tavern (1938-89) separated drought from the
production signal. The same cumulative-departure analysis for 2018-2026 needs a
longer NOAA record than the October 2025 start currently on file. Support is
mixed and incomplete, not absent.

None of these explanations are mutually exclusive, and this proposal's own
calibration and remapping work (Methods, below) is designed to generate the
kind of real, time-paired chemistry and discharge data that could
eventually discriminate between them: it is not designed, on its own, to
settle the question now.

## Chloride discharge as a tracer of geothermal outflow

Michael Sorey's own framing of this system (developed across [@sorey1992],
[@sorey2008], and [@sorey2017]) is the conceptual backbone of this
proposal. Because chloride behaves conservatively in this system (it is
neither added nor removed by mineral reactions or degassing on the way to
discharge), the difference in chloride mass flux between two points on
Steamboat Creek can be used to estimate how much thermal water is entering
the creek between them, without needing to locate or measure every
individual spring or seep along the way. Sorey and Spielman applied this
method at two gauging sites, Rhodes Road (SBRR) and Bella Vista (SBBV),
reporting 730-1,214 gallons per minute for 2007-08 [@sorey2008] and an
average of 60 liters per second (range 45-90 L/s) across 24 sampling events
from 2008 to 2016 [@sorey2017]. A 2026 poster using the same method and
sites, co-authored with Cary Lindsey, asked a single leading question: did
the 2025 Lower Sinter Terrace geysering event represent activation of a new
geothermal source, or redistribution of fluids within an existing
hydrothermal conduit network [@irvinlindsey2026]? That question is the
direct ancestor of this proposal's own central question below. The poster's
own evidence favored redistribution over a new source on two independent
grounds: major-ion chemistry and stable isotopes showed the reactivated
fissure discharging the same hydrothermal fluid already expressed in nearby
springs and wells, and paired temperature loggers at the terrace showed a
strong inverse relationship to each other (r = -0.68): as one logger
warmed, the other cooled, consistent with discharge shifting between vents
within a single connected, shallow, fracture-controlled flow system rather
than a uniform, system-wide change or a chemically distinct new source. The
poster's own chloride-flux calculation put post-eruption thermal inflow at
roughly 27 L/s, below the 2008-2016 average of 60 L/s [@sorey2017], meaning
overall thermal discharge may have declined even as flow paths reorganized.
This proposal's own preliminary results (below) extend that one-time
calculation into a repeatable, database-grounded estimate, and its own
field campaign (also below) finds that the system has kept changing since
the poster was presented.

The practical problem with the chloride-flux method has always been that it
requires discrete water samples, collected and analyzed in a laboratory, at
a temporal resolution most field campaigns cannot sustain for long. This
thesis's central contribution is testing whether continuous,
field-deployable specific-conductance monitoring (already demonstrated as a
workable chloride proxy for geothermal solute flux in Yellowstone's rivers
[@mccleskey2012; @mccleskey2016]) can do the same job at Steamboat, letting
a much sparser chloride-sampling campaign be calibrated against a
continuous conductance record rather than requiring chloride itself to be
sampled at high frequency indefinitely.

## Purpose of study

**How the study is scoped: from the fissure outward.** The work starts at
the fissure, the single most visible and best-documented expression of
the 2025 eruption, where this project holds a paired water sample, a gas
sample, a temperature-logger record, and field photographs. It then
zooms out in steps: first to the other features on the Lower Sinter
Terrace (the resort-tank well, three springs and seeps, and the new hot
spring found in August 2026), asking whether they share the fissure's
deep source and how their chemistry diverges near the surface; then to
Steamboat Creek, where the SBRR and SBGG conductivity loggers and the
chloride mass balance integrate the thermal discharge of the whole
terrace into one measurable signal; and finally to the regional
monitoring network of production, injection, monitoring, and domestic
wells that surrounds it, which supplies the historical baseline and the
context for any change. Each step widens the spatial frame but uses the
same tools, so a result at the fissure can be checked against the same
result at the creek and across the network.

**Central question.** Can continuous conductivity measurements be
used to accurately estimate chloride discharge and geothermal outflow
at Steamboat Hills, and what do those measurements reveal about
hydrothermal-system evolution following the 2025 eruption?

This proposal is organized around four research questions, each with
its own concrete deliverable.

**RQ1: How stable is the chloride-conductivity relationship through time
and across site types?** Does a single calibration apply everywhere, or do
outlet, creek, monitoring-well, and spring waters each require their own
relationship, and how much uncertainty results from seasonal and temporal
variation? *Deliverable:* one or more real chloride-to-conductance
calibration equations, with stated uncertainty.

**RQ2: What is the minimum chloride-sampling frequency required to maintain
a scientifically defensible, conductivity-based estimate of chloride
flux?** *Deliverable:* a quantitative monitoring-design recommendation,
developed through the Monte Carlo analysis described in the Methods section
below.

**RQ3: Are conductivity variations driven primarily by conservative mixing,
or by geochemical reactions that would decouple conductance from
chloride?** Is chloride itself behaving conservatively here? Is
conductivity? Are mineral reactions altering conductance independently of
chloride concentration? *Deliverable:* a geochemical, PHREEQC-based
physical justification (or an explicit, documented limitation) for the
chloride-conductivity proxy.

**RQ4: Has geothermal outflow at Steamboat changed following the 2025
eruption?** *Deliverable:* a post-eruption interpretation of chloride flux,
conservative-tracer ratios, and outlet chemistry, read against the 70-year
discharge record Sorey and others established.

**Working hypotheses.** Going into the data, the expectation for each
question is: (RQ1) a single calibration will not fit every site type
equally well, since outlet, creek, monitoring-well, and spring waters
are exposed to different near-surface conditions, but the relationship
should hold within a given site type; (RQ2) daily-to-weekly chloride
sampling should be sufficient to keep a conductivity-based estimate
defensible, with the open question being exactly where that
breaks down, not whether a workable frequency exists; (RQ3) chloride
should behave conservatively everywhere, but conductance will likely
decouple from it to some degree wherever carbonate dissolution or
precipitation is active, which PHREEQC modeling should be able to
flag; (RQ4) thermal-water chloride has probably declined somewhat
since the 1950-1991 baseline, consistent with decades of production,
but the thermal source's own conservative Cl/B signature should be
essentially unchanged.

**Why this is a multi-component study, and why that matters.** The four
research questions above are not independent side projects stapled
together; each one supplies a piece the others need. Aqueous major-ion
and isotope chemistry identifies the thermal end-member and tests whether
mixing is conservative (RQ1, RQ3). Fissure gas chemistry and
PHREEQC-based geochemical modeling provide an independent cross-check on
reservoir temperature and reaction state that water chemistry alone
cannot give (RQ3, RQ4). Hydrology (stream discharge, water levels, and
the chloride mass-balance method itself) converts a concentration into a
flux, the quantity that actually answers whether outflow has changed
(RQ4). Time-series statistics (autocorrelation-aware cross-validation,
Monte Carlo subsampling) turn a continuous conductance record and a
sparse chloride record into a defensible, quantified sampling design
(RQ2). And the chloride-conductivity proxy statistics (RQ1) are the hinge
that lets the other three legs of the project feed a single, continuously
updated monitoring tool instead of remaining a one-time snapshot. No
single one of these methods, used alone, could answer the central
question; used together, and built on top of the same relational
database and the same reproducible scripts, they let a sparse, expensive
field campaign and a continuous, cheap sensor record check each other
rather than being read in isolation. If the chloride-conductivity proxy
holds up, this combination is also what turns a single thesis into a
durable, reusable monitoring framework rather than another one-time
estimate: the same database, scripts, and calibration can be re-applied
the next time this system changes, by whoever is managing it then.

# Background: chloride, conductivity, and the role of geochemical modeling

## Chloride and specific conductance as conservative-tracer proxies

Steamboat's thermal water is a sodium-chloride-dominated fluid; meteoric
(background) water in the same area is dilute and comparatively richer in
calcium and magnesium. Chloride's conservative behavior in this system is
what makes it usable both as a tracer of thermal-water fraction in an
individual sample, and, by mass balance against stream discharge, as an
estimate of total thermal-water discharge [@sorey1992; @sorey2008;
@sorey2017]. Specific conductance is proposed as a proxy for chloride, not
because conductance is itself the quantity of scientific interest, but
because it is inexpensive, continuous, and field-deployable in a way
discrete chloride sampling is not. Whether that substitution actually holds
at Steamboat (across sites, seasons, and the period before and after the
2025 eruption) is this proposal's central empirical question. This proposal
tests that substitution directly; it does not assume the answer in advance.


## Major-ion chemistry: what each analyte tells us

| Analyte | Role in this system |
|---|---|
| Chloride | The primary conservative tracer. |
| Sodium, potassium | Track with chloride in the real thermal end-member; also the basis of sodium/potassium geothermometry (below). |
| Sulfate | Also strongly correlated with chloride, sodium, and potassium here (a secondary conservative-ish tracer, though sulfate can be affected by anhydrite/gypsum equilibria at high enough concentration). |
| Calcium, magnesium | Behave oppositely to the chloride/sodium/potassium group; track a more dilute, rock-reacted water-rock interaction signature. |
| Alkalinity | Drives carbonate mineral saturation (calcite, dolomite, aragonite). |
| Boron, lithium, fluoride | Minor conservative-ish tracers used for independent cross-checks, such as the chloride-to-boron ratio discussed below. |
| Silica | The basis of quartz/chalcedony geothermometry; behaves less conservatively than sodium/potassium on the ascent-to-discharge path at Steamboat. |

## Charge balance and mineral saturation

Every water analysis is first screened for internal consistency via
the standard charge-balance-error statistic,

$$
\text{CBE\%} = \frac{\sum z_i m_i^{\text{cation}} - \sum |z_i| m_i^{\text{anion}}}
{\sum z_i m_i^{\text{cation}} + \sum |z_i| m_i^{\text{anion}}} \times 100,
$$

where $z_i$ and $m_i$ are the charge and molar concentration of each
ion; a sample passing within $\pm 5\%$ is analytically reliable
enough to model further. The mineral saturation index then
quantifies how far a water is from equilibrium with a given mineral,

$$
SI = \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{IAP}{K_{sp}}\right),
$$

where $IAP$ is the ion activity product computed from the sample's
speciated chemistry and $K_{sp}$ is that mineral's temperature-
dependent solubility product; $SI = 0$ is equilibrium, $SI > 0$
implies a tendency to precipitate (scale), and $SI < 0$ implies a
tendency to dissolve.

## Geothermometry: two independent, and divergent, temperature estimates

Activity-based sodium/potassium geothermometers estimate the deep
reservoir temperature a water last equilibrated with, from the ratio
of sodium to potassium activity. Two widely used forms are
Giggenbach's [@giggenbach1988]

$$
T_{\text{Gigg}}(^\circ C) = \frac{1390}{1.75 + \log_{10}(a_{Na}/a_K)} - 273.15
$$

and Fournier's [@fournier1979]

$$
T_{\text{Four}}(^\circ C) = \frac{1217}{1.483 + \log_{10}(a_{Na}/a_K)} - 273.15 .
$$

Silica (quartz/chalcedony) geothermometry instead uses dissolved
silica's own temperature-dependent solubility, read from the real
equilibrium temperature at which a mineral's saturation index crosses
zero. At Steamboat, sodium/potassium estimates (154-256 degrees
Celsius) systematically and substantially exceed quartz/chalcedony
estimates (52-127 degrees Celsius). This divergence is real and
informative, not a contradiction: silica re-
equilibrates toward ambient conditions faster than the sodium/
potassium ratio does as water cools and dilutes on its way to
discharge, so the two geothermometers are expected to diverge exactly
this way along a single cooling, diluting flow path. This
divergence-as-evidence approach follows Shevenell and De Rocher's
[@shevenell2005] own evaluation of multiple geothermometers across
several Nevada geothermal power plants, which found that no single
geothermometer is reliable in isolation and that comparing several
against each other is itself diagnostic of a system's mixing and
cooling history, not just a single reservoir-temperature estimate.

## How PHREEQC will be used: a supporting mechanism, not a modeling thesis

PHREEQC [@phreeqc] is a widely used, open-source geochemical modeling
program that solves aqueous speciation, mineral saturation, mixing,
and inverse mass-balance problems from a water analysis and a chosen
thermodynamic database. This proposal deliberately does **not** treat
PHREEQC as a standalone geochemical-modeling exercise producing
saturation-index tables for their own sake. Instead, PHREEQC answers
four specific questions that directly serve the chloride-conductivity
proxy question above.

**Objective 1: Define water types.** Combine major-ion chemistry, principal
component analysis, and hydrochemical facies clustering with PHREEQC's own
fluid classification to separate real samples into a thermal end-member
(outlet and thermal-well samples), mixed waters (for example, monitoring
wells with evidence of partial dilution), and dilute background waters
(domestic wells with no thermal signature).

**Objective 2: Evaluate whether conductivity is behaving conservatively.**
The core question is why conductance should track chloride at all. PHREEQC
is used to test whether carbonate precipitation, silica precipitation, ion
exchange, or evaporation could be altering conductance independently of
chloride: summarized as a real table of which processes can alter chloride,
which can alter conductance, and whether the two are expected to move
together or diverge. This table is the direct physical justification for,
or documented limitation of, the proxy relationship RQ1 and RQ3 depend on.

**Objective 3: Test thermal end-member stability across decades.** Real
chemistry exists from the 1950s, the 1990s, and the present. Each era's
thermal samples are run through PHREEQC's own equilibrium calculations (not
just raw concentration ratios) to ask whether the end-member's equilibrium
behavior, not only its composition, has remained stable: a question
directly relevant to whether a calibration fit today should be expected to
hold if extrapolated backward or forward in time.

**Objective 4: Investigate calibration outliers.** Any real
chloride-conductance calibration will have outliers. Rather than discard
them, PHREEQC is used to ask why a given sample deviates (dilution, mineral
precipitation, mixing with a different water, or an unusual pH), which is a
more informative use of the modeling capability than reporting saturation
indices in isolation.

## What PHREEQC can and cannot tell us: a batch tool, not reactive transport

In plain terms, PHREEQC answers one specific kind of question: if this
water sits in contact with these minerals and this gas, what does its
chemistry settle into? It does not need to know, and cannot tell us, where
in the ground that water actually is, how fast it is moving, or how far it
has to travel to get there. Every PHREEQC calculation used in this proposal
(speciation, saturation index, mixing, the forward reaction-path titration)
treats a water sample as a single, well-mixed parcel reacting for as long
as needed to reach the modeled result, not as a parcel of water moving
through real rock over real time and real distance. This is usually called
a *batch* model (some use *zero-dimensional*), to distinguish it from a
*reactive-transport* model, which adds a real spatial grid and a real flow
field (how fast and in which direction water moves between grid cells), so
that chemistry can be tracked as it actually happens at a specific place
and time while water moves through real rock. Reactive-transport tools do
exist, including a version of PHREEQC's own chemistry engine coupled to a
three-dimensional flow model (PHAST, built by the same United States
Geological Survey group), alongside other established codes (for example
TOUGHREACT, CrunchFlow). None of those is used here. The reason is not that
PHREEQC itself is incapable of this in principle (PHAST proves it is not),
but that running any of them responsibly needs a calibrated permeability
field, effective porosity, defined reservoir boundary conditions, and a
transient pressure history, none of which currently exist for Steamboat at
the resolution a reactive-transport model would need. Attempting one now
would produce a model dominated by untested assumptions rather than real
constraints.

This distinction matters for how every PHREEQC result in this proposal
should be read, not just as a technical footnote. When the forward
reaction-path titration (Chapter 4) finds a sample best explained by a net
dissolution of roughly one-tenth of a millimole of calcite and dolomite,
that is a real, quantitative statement about how much carbonate chemistry
needed to be added or removed to match the sample: it is not a statement
about *where* that dissolution happened, over what distance, or how long it
took. Likewise, a two-end-member mixing fraction says what proportion of
two chemically distinct waters would explain a sample's chloride; it says
nothing about the physical flow path the water actually followed to arrive
there.

Despite that limitation, the results in this proposal are not reduced to
the point of being uninformative: they draw a genuinely useful, if
spatially blind, distinction, and the clearest example is already in hand.
A batch model with no spatial information at all is still able to show that
SBS_0001's chemistry cannot be explained by the same simple
mixing-plus-carbonate-reaction model that explains its four real
downgradient neighbors (Chapter 4), even though SBS_0001 and one of those
neighbors sit only 109 meters apart. That is exactly the kind of specific
finding a batch geochemical model is built to deliver (a genuine chemical
distinction between two samples) and exactly the kind of finding it cannot,
by itself, explain physically: a fault, a locally different flow path, and
a locally different rock unit are all equally consistent candidate
explanations for that same chemical result, and only real spatial and
structural data (the next section) could ever distinguish between them. A
three-dimensional geologic model is still a genuine and valuable part of
this work, but strictly as **conceptual geologic context** (a real,
well-grounded picture of where production, injection, and monitoring wells
sit relative to known structure and lithology) not as a platform for
simulating fluid movement. That distinction is maintained consistently
throughout the Methods section below.

# Previous work

Steamboat is among the most thoroughly studied geothermal systems in the
western United States, with continuous published work since the 1860s.
This chapter organizes that record by what each body of work established,
so the contribution of this proposal is clear against it: first the
geologic and structural framework, then the hydrology and chloride-discharge
record that this thesis directly extends, then the subsurface and
monitoring-network studies, the gas and geochemical datasets, the
operator-scale reservoir work, and finally the 2022-2026 reawakening
itself. @tbl-pubtimeline lists the same literature in publication order.

## Geologic and structural framework

White, Thompson, and Sandberg [@white1964b; @thompsonwhite1964]
established the geologic framework still used today: a Mesozoic
metamorphic basement intruded by Cretaceous granitic rocks, buried under
more than a hundred cubic miles of mostly andesitic Cenozoic volcanic
rock, and cut by the basin-and-range Steamboat Springs fault zone. White
argued that this fault zone localizes the present thermal area simply
because it is the lowest-elevation fault available for deep thermal water
to intersect the water table, not because it has any special structural
property. His interpretation of the heat source (a large, roughly 50
km^3, slowly cooling magma chamber supplying heat by conduction for at
least 100,000 years, with "no new magma... directly involved" and
volcanic steam contributing under five percent of total system water
[@white1964b]) frames Steamboat as a persistent, long-lived convective
system rather than one newly activated by fresh input, which bears
directly on this proposal's redistribution-versus-new-source question.
Arehart and others [@arehart2003] and Johnson and Hulen [@johnsonhulen2006]
later brought trace-element and gas evidence for a magmatic heat source,
a partly differing view that agrees on the point that matters here: the
heat source is long-lived, not newly arrived. Silberman and others
[@silberman1979] constrained the duration of hydrothermal activity from
spatially associated volcanic rocks.

White's own record also shows that dramatic surface behavior is not new at
Steamboat. He compiled published observations of episodic natural
geysering extending back to 1860-1862 (De Quille, 1876, "the first
published record of geyser observations in the United States"
[@white1968c]) and accounts of drilling-induced eruptions through the
early twentieth century (Lindgren, 1903-1905; Jones, 1912-1914; Gianella,
1939, wells erupting stibnite from depth) [@white1964b]. A 1947-48
Low Terrace well that erupted continuously once drilling intersected its
aquifer is a direct historical analog to the 2025 pipe eruption. The 2025
event is therefore the latest instance of a long-documented pattern, not
an unprecedented one. Vaughan and others [@vaughan2005] later mapped the
surface mineral expression with airborne thermal-infrared imagery,
distinguishing actively forming opaline sinter from older chalcedony
sinter and an acid-sulfate alteration halo around the fumaroles, which
is the kind of surface evidence this proposal's remapping is designed to
update for the post-eruption terrace.

Collar [@collar1990thesis; also Collar and Huntley, @collar1990] contributed the fault and air-photo-
lineament map this thesis treats as its best candidate for the
structural context: it also locates several wells already resolved in
this project's database, which gives natural control points for
digitizing. Skalbeck [@skalbeck2001] supplied the most detailed
geophysical subsurface characterization, interpreting depths to the
principal units (alluvium, volcanic rock, and the altered cap of the
granodiorite bedrock body) along geophysical survey lines, and
tabulating a multi-decade well-monitoring record.

## Hydrology and the chloride-discharge record

This is the body of work the thesis directly extends. White [@white1968c]
measured chloride as a conservative tracer for total system heat flow,
reporting a pre-boiling upflow of 800-820 ppm at about 175 C, and
estimated a roughly 100 gpm thermal inflow to the creek along the Low
Terrace that is not visible at the surface. Sorey and Colvard
[@sorey1992], an administrative report for the Bureau of Land Management,
is the single most detailed historical baseline: it documents the
near-total cessation of natural spring flow at the main and low terraces
between 1986 and 1989 and attributes most, though not all, of it to
regional shallow-groundwater drawdown rather than to production; it
tabulates 1950-1991 chemistry for nine features, a Cl/B ratio near 19 in
1990-91 thermal samples, barometric efficiencies of 0.42-0.45 at two
springs, aquifer-test results, and a chloride mass balance that treats an
820 mg/L thermal and 6 mg/L non-thermal end-member as the two components
of Steamboat Creek flow. Collar's M.S. thesis [@collar1990thesis], written
from the same USGS grant study, applied the same chloride-flux logic to
1988-89 discharge measurements, 35 years before this proposal's version of
it, and is treated in detail below. Sorey [@sorey2000]
found that groundwater levels had recovered by 2000 while spring flow
had not resumed, the critical observation that recovery alone did not
reactivate the terrace. Sorey and Spielman [@sorey2008; @sorey2017]
refined the chloride-mass-balance method at two Steamboat Creek gauging
sites, Rhodes Road (SBRR) and Bella Vista (SBBV), reporting 730-1,214
gallons per minute for 2007-08 and an average of 60 liters per second
(range 45-90 L/s) across 24 sampling events from 2008 to 2016. Cohen and
Loeltz [@cohenloeltz1964] characterized Truckee Meadows groundwater
outside the field, providing background for several wells this proposal
uses for its barometric-efficiency calculation.

Collar's thesis [@collar1990thesis] is the most complete single treatment of
the 1986-89 decline and the closest methodological predecessor of this
proposal. Over 1986-89 he logged water levels in about a dozen main- and
low-terrace spring vents, strat and observation wells, and private alluvial
wells, gaged Steamboat Creek, Galena Creek, and the ditches at 63 stations in
three surveys (June-July 1988, August 1988, March 1989), and tested earthquakes, barometric pressure, earth tides,
precipitation, a nearby spa well, and geothermal production as candidate
causes. He concluded that discharging wells in the CPI field, and to a much
lesser degree the OESI field, were the principal cause of the decline, on the
grounds that spring levels fell during production and recovered during
shut-ins, many springs moved in parallel, spring hydrographs mimicked those of
observation wells known to be connected to the production wells, and natural
thermal discharge to the creek had fallen. Sorey and Colvard [@sorey1992],
working on the same period and drawing on overlapping data, reached a
different weighting: 80-95 percent of the roughly 17 ft head decline beneath
the main terrace attributed to shallow South Truckee Meadows groundwater
decline and only 1-3 ft (5-20 percent) to the CPI field. The two analyses
agree on the facts that matter most for this proposal: the CPI field is
hydraulically connected to strat wells 2 and 9, heads beneath the terrace
fell by about 17 ft, and drought alone does not explain the decline. They
disagree on how much of the head loss was caused by production, which is
exactly the kind of attribution question that a pressure or injection
change would raise again, and it remains unresolved.

Collar's creek work uses the same two-end-member chloride balance as this
proposal (thermal water 820 mg/L, nonthermal 4 mg/L), with explicit
equations for gaining and losing reaches, and divides the creek at Virginia
City Highway (Geiger Grade) into a "geothermal area" reach and a South
Truckee Meadows reach extending to Huffaker Hills. His June 1988 and March
1989 surveys put thermal inflow to the creek at 490-530 and 660 gpm,
about 60 to 80 percent of White's 1955 value, with the shortfall concentrated
near the main and low terraces (about 60 percent of 1955) rather than
downstream (about 80 percent). He also records that Shump's earlier estimate
[@shump1985], made with specific conductivity, changed substantially when its
nonthermal end-member was set consistently with White's chloride value,
because specific conductivity and chloride are not directly related in the
carbonate- and bicarbonate-dominated nonthermal groundwater of the South
Truckee Meadows. That is a documented precedent for the failure mode this
proposal's conductance-proxy test is designed to detect. Two further results
bear directly on the Lower Sinter Terrace. First, during 1989 an intermittently
pumped well at the Steamboat Spa, about 2,800 ft south of the main terrace,
produced weekday drawdown spikes and weekend recoveries in well GS-1 and the
old spa well on the low terrace and lowered spring 50, while main-terrace
springs 6 and 12 did not respond, so the low terrace is hydraulically
sensitive to nearby withdrawal in a way the main terrace is not. Second, of
twenty low-terrace springs White cataloged (nine of them geysers), only spring
50 was still flowing (about 3 gpm) in 1988, and spring 50 was the one spring
where Nehring found young meteoric water mixing with thermal water in 1977.

## Monitoring network, gas chemistry, and early geochemistry

Klein, Johnson, and Spielman [@klein2007] documented the groundwater and
geothermal monitor-well network in detail, providing the well-identity
framework that much of this proposal's site resolution depends on.
Mariner and Janik [@mariner1995] provide an independent, contemporaneous
geochemical dataset and conceptual model, including gas chemistry that
this proposal's geothermometer cross-validation draws on, and Nehring
[@nehring1979] produced an early reservoir-temperature estimate from
enthalpy-chloride and deuterium-chloride diagrams on 1977 spring samples,
directly comparable to this proposal's own geothermometer results.

## Reservoir and operator-scale work

Reservoir-scale studies situate this proposal's surface and shallow
focus within the operator's larger picture: a numerical model update
spanning forty years of production [@dhakal2025], a three-dimensional
reservoir model calibrated against more than 130 wells [@bjornsson2014],
and a directional-drilling account for well 83C-6ST1 that supplies this
proposal's only non-vertical well survey [@akerley2021]. State and
federal agency records (the Nevada Divisions of Environmental Protection,
Minerals, and Water Resources, and the U.S. Geological Survey) supply the
production-well chemistry, permit, well-construction, and streamflow
records that extend this baseline into the present monitoring period.

## The 2022-2026 reawakening

Lindsey and others [@lindsey2026] published the first full account of
the 2022-2025 reawakening and the June 2025 eruption, tracing the stages
from renewed diffuse steaming to discrete seeps and vents to the
eruption itself, and documenting that capping the well did not stop
discharge but redistributed it laterally. This project's own preliminary
chloride-discharge estimate following the eruption, co-authored with
Lindsey, was presented as a poster at the 2026 Geothermal Rising
Conference in Houston, Texas [@irvinlindsey2026]. It found major-ion and
isotope chemistry at the fissure matching nearby springs and wells, an
inverse correlation between paired terrace temperature loggers
(r = -0.68), and a thermal inflow of about 27 L/s against the 2008-2016
average of 60 L/s, and it concluded that the evidence favored
redistribution within an existing conduit network over a new source.
This proposal turns that one-time estimate into a repeatable,
database-grounded one and tests the conclusion against more data.

# Methods and plan of action

## Monitoring network and supporting database

Every method described below draws on field sampling at the Lower Sinter
Terrace; state-agency chemistry, permit, well-construction, and
water-rights records; federal streamflow, water-level, weather, and
historical specific-conductance records; and historical literature
chemistry that has been transcribed directly from Sorey and Colvard
[@sorey1992], Mariner and Janik [@mariner1995], and Skalbeck
[@skalbeck2001] rather than merely cited. These sources are integrated into
a single, queryable database (1,600 samples across 269 wells and additional
spring, seep, and creek locations, as of this writing) rather than kept as
separate spreadsheets, specifically so that a question spanning multiple
decades and multiple agencies' worth of records can be answered
consistently rather than re-assembled by hand each time it is asked. A
standing data-quality process checks for missing values, implausible
readings, and internal consistency on an ongoing basis. One concrete
example materially affects the preliminary results below: a missing
alkalinity parameter in one major chemistry feed initially made
charge-balance error look far worse than it really was (roughly 60%). Once
corrected, the median charge-balance error for the same samples dropped to
about 0.7%, with most samples now passing the standard plus-or-minus-5%
quality threshold.

**Spring and well remapping.** Several springs at the Lower Sinter
Terrace are listed in the operator's own records as inactive. A
central field task of this thesis is walking that terrace and
confirming, for each one, whether it is in fact dry, seeping, or
actively discharging. This fieldwork has so far produced 51 real,
GPS-tagged survey points at the terrace (28 seeps, 13 steaming-ground
observations, 7 springs, and 3 creek points).

**Chemistry and isotope sampling.** Water samples are collected at springs,
wells, and creek stations, with field parameters (pH, temperature, specific
conductance) measured at the time of collection and laboratory analyses
(major ions, alkalinity, trace elements, and delta-18-O/delta-D isotopes)
run afterward. This project's own field campaign has collected 71 real
water samples to date.

**Temperature logger network.** Eleven continuous temperature
loggers are deployed at springs, wells, and along the eruption
fissure itself, giving a direct, continuous view of whether the 2025
eruption's thermal signature has been stable, cooling, or shifting
laterally since the wellhead was capped.

**Conductivity loggers as a chloride proxy.** Two continuous specific-
conductance loggers were deployed in Steamboat Creek on July 15, 2026: one
co-located with the existing U.S. Geological Survey gauge near Rhodes
Road (the upstream/control site) and one further downstream near
Geiger Grade, matching the same two site roles Sorey and Spielman used
for their own chloride-flux calculations [@sorey2008; @sorey2017].

@fig-sbgg-install shows the downstream (SBGG) logger shortly after
installation in July 2026: the specific-conductance/temperature
sensor housed inside the white PVC pipe, with a yellow transect line
marking the cross-section used for repeat discharge measurements.

```{r fig-sbgg-install}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/field_photo_sbgg_install.jpg",
  "The SBGG (Geiger Grade) continuous specific-conductance logger, housed in the white PVC pipe at center, shortly after installation in Steamboat Creek (yellow line marks the discharge-measurement transect; capture date not preserved in this file).",
  alt = "Photograph of a white PVC logger housing standing in a shallow creek, with a yellow transect line and streamside willows.",
  id = "fig-sbgg-install"
)
```

**An extended conductivity record and a known retrieval artifact.** Both
stream conductivity loggers (SBRR and SBGG) were re-downloaded October 12,
2026, extending the continuous record from 2026-08-22 through 2026-10-10.
Whenever a logger is removed from the stream to connect a shuttle and then
relaunched, it reads ambient air instead of stream water, producing a
sharp, implausible drop in specific conductance at the retrieval and
relaunch moments (@fig-conductivity-timeseries). A detector added to this
project's conductivity QC script flags those readings automatically
(`qc_flag = 'field_visit_disturbance'`); applied retroactively it
reproduces every previously hand-flagged row.

The flagged points mark only what the detector can see, and they
understate the problem. Field observations indicate that each logger sat
in air inside its housing for at least several days before each pull, as
the stream dropped away from the sensor. That earlier interval is not
separable from real stream signal in the conductance record: at both
sites the daily conductance stays smooth through the final days before the
2026-10-10 pull, and the daily temperature range widens only slightly
(a weak and non-diagnostic hint, since air temperature also drives it). The
orange points should therefore not be read as bounding the period of
valid data. Readings from the days immediately preceding any retrieval
are treated as provisional, and the calibration and Monte Carlo analyses
below will be re-run with a conservative pre-retrieval exclusion window
once the actual duration of exposure is established from field notes and
the next download.

```{r fig-conductivity-timeseries}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/conductivity_timeseries.png",
  "SBRR and SBGG conductivity record, 2026-07-15 to 2026-10-10. Orange points are readings the QC detector flagged at retrieval and relaunch events; the dashed line marks the last flagged reading. They do not bound the longer interval before each pull when the sensor sat partly or fully out of flowing water, which is not detectable in the conductance record.",
  alt = "Two-panel time series of specific conductance at SBGG and SBRR with orange points flagging readings at two retrieval events and dashed lines at the last flagged reading.",
  id = "fig-conductivity-timeseries"
)
```

@tbl-fieldtogis summarizes how this project's field mapping and the
historically documented wells and springs all flow through the same
database into the same GIS export, a single traceable path from a GPS point
in the field to a layer a committee member could open in ArcGIS.

```{r tbl-fieldtogis}
field_tbl <- read.csv("data/derived/monitoring_network/fieldwork_to_database_to_gis_summary.csv")
names(field_tbl) <- c("Source", "N", "Detail", "Database tables", "In GIS export?")
field_tbl[["Database tables"]] <- gsub("_", " ", gsub("/", ", ", field_tbl[["Database tables"]]))
field_tbl[["In GIS export?"]] <- gsub("_", " ", field_tbl[["In GIS export?"]])
knitr::kable(
  field_tbl, row.names = FALSE, align = c("l", "c", "l", "l", "l"),
  caption = "Field mapping and historically documented locations, traced from source through this project's database to the GeoPackage GIS export."
)
```

## Seasonal variation: the regional monitoring network compared to the Lower Sinter Terrace flowpath

The monitoring network described above carries real construction detail
(screened/completion interval, elevation, total depth) that the Lower
Sinter Terrace flowpath samples themselves currently do not: a real, stated
asymmetry worth making explicit before comparing them, shown in
@tbl-wellconstruction: SBF_0001, SBW_0001, SBW_0002, and the three real
springs/seep have no `Wells` record at all (no elevation, no completion
interval, no total depth on file), while STMGID MW3/MW10 and several of the
real U230-round monitoring wells do. One real unit inconsistency is
flagged, not silently fixed: Herz Domestic Well's own completion interval
(12-34) is stored in meters, a Skalbeck (2001)-era holdover, while every
other well in this table is in feet: a reminder to check units before
comparing completion depths directly across sources.

```{r tbl-wellconstruction}
well_tbl <- read.csv("data/derived/monitoring_network/monitoring_well_construction_summary.csv")
knitr::kable(
  well_tbl, digits = 1, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Well", "Elevation (m)", "Total depth", "Top perforation", "Bottom perforation"),
  caption = "Real construction data on file for the regional monitoring network. Units are feet except Herz Domestic Well's completion interval (meters, flagged in text)."
)
```

Within that network, five real and relevant field-parameter rounds (late
September through December 2025, extended here with the earlier August 2025
round) at the eight monitoring/domestic wells plus the injection-side
outlets, shown in @fig-fieldchem, give a real picture of how much specific
conductance, pH, and temperature actually move season to season at wells
well outside the terrace itself: some outlets swing by more than 1,500
microsiemens per centimeter across the five rounds, while others (the
shallow domestic wells) stay comparatively flat. Water levels tell a
related story, shown in @fig-wlstandardized: standardizing each well's own
depth-to-water to its own mean and standard deviation over the same real
window shows Herz Domestic Well tracking STMGID MW3 closely (r roughly
0.94, p roughly 0.005, n=6), but not STMGID MW10 (r roughly -0.57, not
significant): consistent with MW3's much shorter, shallower screened
interval (100 feet, 186-286 feet) sharing more of a common shallow signal
with Herz Domestic than MW10's 480-foot, much deeper interval does.

```{r fig-fieldchem}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/monthly_indicator_timeline/monthly_indicator_timeline_field_chemistry.png",
  "Monthly mean specific conductance, pH, and temperature at monitoring and domestic wells (blue), plant outlet and injection-side taps (orange), and this project's 2026 terrace and creek samples (green), July 2025-May 2026. One thin line per site; sites with a single month appear as points.",
  alt = "Three-panel time series of conductivity, pH, and temperature at 29 sites, colored by three site groups, July 2025 through May 2026.",
  id = "fig-fieldchem"
)
```

```{r fig-wlstandardized}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/monthly_indicator_timeline/water_level_field_vs_stmgid_standardized.png",
  "Standardized (z-score) water-level trajectories, five real monitoring wells, June-December 2025.",
  alt = "Line plot of standardized water-level z-scores for five wells over six months, showing Herz Domestic Well tracking STMGID MW3 more closely than STMGID MW10.",
  id = "fig-wlstandardized"
)
```

Compared directly against this, the terrace's own real seasonal record (the
SBRR/SBGG conductivity loggers, @fig-conductivity-timeseries above) covers
a different year's window (July-October 2026, not the 2025 monitoring-round
window above) (stated plainly rather than implying a literal same-time
comparison), but shows a comparatively modest relative swing (roughly
330-370 microsiemens per centimeter at SBRR, 1,040-1,130 at SBGG) against
the same backdrop of some regional monitoring wells swinging by a factor of
two or more across their own five real rounds. Read together with the
construction-data asymmetry above, the honest statement is that the
regional network already shows real, well-dependent seasonal variability
large enough to matter for any future flowpath comparison, while the
flowpath wells/springs themselves still need their own construction data
and a real, overlapping-window seasonal record before that comparison can
be made directly rather than by rough analogy.

## Historical comparison: chloride and temperature at previously documented wells and springs

A separate, complementary comparison asks the same stability question
RQ4 asks of the thermal end-member, but across a wider set of real,
individually named wells and springs rather than one pooled average:
seventeen real sites with independently sourced chloride records, twelve
spanning more than one sampling campaign (Sorey and Colvard
[-@sorey1992], Mariner and Janik [-@mariner1995], Skalbeck's
[-@skalbeck2001] 1985-1998 monthly monitoring, and NDEP) plus five wells whose only chloride values are 2024 NDEP Public Records Request samples, shown
side by side in @fig-histcl and @fig-histtemp.

```{r fig-histcl}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/historical_cl_by_well.png",
  "Chloride through time at seventeen historically documented wells and springs, every measurement on file. The bottom five panels (Boyd Domestic, Eich, Jeppson Geothermal, Rogers Domestic, Soccer Field) hold two 2024 NDEP Public Records Request samples each; panels use independent y-axes.",
  alt = "Seventeen-panel scatter and line plot of chloride over time, one panel per well or spring, with sparse 2024 points at five wells.",
  id = "fig-histcl"
)
```

```{r fig-histtemp}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/historical_temperature_by_well.png",
  "Temperature through time at the same sites, every field-measured value on file (sites with no field temperature record have no panel data).",
  alt = "Multi-panel scatter and line plot of field-measured temperature over time, one panel per well or spring.",
  id = "fig-histtemp"
)
```

The pattern is not uniform decline, and not uniform stability: several
wells (Herz Domestic, Brown's School, Flame, Pine Tree Ranch-1) show a
real, substantial chloride AND temperature RISE together through the late
1980s and early 1990s, both parameters moving the same direction at the
same time, before Herz Domestic and Brown's School both decline again by
the late 1990s. This is a genuinely different pattern from the thermal
end-member's own near-constant Cl/B ratio over the same decades (above):
individual wells on the margin of the thermal field can show a real, large,
multi-year rise and fall in absolute thermal signature even while the deep
source's own conservative-ratio signature stays essentially fixed,
consistent with these wells sampling a variable mixing zone rather than the
source itself. Steinhardt shows the opposite, already-documented pattern (a
real decline from 300 to roughly 140 mg/L between 1987 and 1990) while
GS-5, 23-5, and Cox I-1 (all closer to the historic core of the field) stay
comparatively high and stable across their own, shorter real records.

The five NDEP Public Records Request wells give the only present-day anchors
in the figure, each with two samples (March and June 2024). They span the
full range of conditions in the network: Eich (530-590 mg/L) and Soccer
Field (470-570 mg/L) carry a clear thermal chloride signature, Boyd (39-45
mg/L) is dilute, and Jeppson (11 mg/L) and Rogers (7 mg/L) are
background-like. Two samples in four months cannot show a trend, so these
points locate each well on the thermal-to-dilute spectrum today rather than
testing drift. NDOT and Herz Deep, sampled for field parameters in 2025,
have no laboratory chloride on file yet and are not plotted; the NDEP data
request in `docs/action_items_for_user.md` is aimed at closing that gap.

None of the seventeen sites above are inside the Lower Sinter Terrace itself,
and none have anything like this multi-decade baseline for the real springs
and seep this project's own fieldwork has confirmed (SBS_0001, SBS_0002,
SBS_0003) or for the new hot spring found in August 2026: those are known
from a single real field season, not seventy years of repeat sampling. That
asymmetry is itself a concrete argument for the ongoing spring and well
remapping and the proposed sampling plan above: without a comparable real
multi-year record at the terrace itself, there is no way yet to tell
whether its own springs would show the same kind of multi-year
rise-and-fall several of these historically-documented wells do, or would
instead track the thermal end-member's own apparent stability: a real,
open, and directly testable question this proposal's monitoring plan is
positioned to answer going forward.

## Monitoring network: 1986-89 compared with the present

Collar's thesis [@collar1990thesis] documents the monitoring network that was
in place when the main-terrace springs failed, and it is the most direct
yardstick for the one assembled here. In 1986-89 the network was dense at the
spring vents and in bedrock: water levels in about a dozen main- and
low-terrace spring vents, in strat wells 2, 5, 9, 13, and 14, in GS-1, GS-8,
and an old spa well on the low terrace, in OESI wells OW-1, OW-2, and IW-1,
and in private alluvial wells (Steinhardt, Brown School, Herz 2, Pine Tree
Ranch-1, and others), with chloride and boron at several of them, plus
stream gaging at 63 stations. Today's network is denser in continuous
temperature and conductance (a dozen temperature loggers, some since lost, and two stream
conductivity loggers) and has modern laboratory chemistry and gas data, but it
has no current water level in the strat wells or the production reservoir, and
no spring-vent water levels at all: the two gaps Collar and Sorey and Colvard
both identified as limiting what could be concluded. @tbl-oldnew sets recent
values beside the older ones, quantity by quantity, with the comparability
limit stated in each row.

| Quantity | 1950s-1989 (Collar; Sorey and Colvard; sources they compile) | Recent / this project | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| Thermal discharge to the creek (creek inflow only) | White 1955: 810 gpm (51 L/s). Collar: 490-530 gpm (31-33 L/s) in 6/88; 660 gpm (42 L/s) in 3/89, about 60-80 percent of 1955 | Sorey and Spielman: 730-1,214 gpm (2007-08), 60 L/s average (2008-16); poster: 27 L/s; database 5/1/2026: 58.7 L/s (one date) | Discharge was low in the late 1980s and back in the 1955 range by 2007; the 2026 single-date value is within the 2008-16 range and the poster average is below it. Reaches and methods differ (see text). |
| Chloride, Rhodes Road (upstream control) | S10: 17.2 mg/L (8/88), 23.8 mg/L (3/89) | NDEP SB5: median 14 mg/L, range 6-72 (n = 143, 1987-2024); SBRR 17.1 mg/L (5/2026) | Indistinguishable across 38 years; no sign of drift at the upstream control. |
| Chloride, Geiger Grade reach | S70: 139, 418, 130 mg/L (6/88, 8/88, 3/89); station match provisional | NDEP SB7: median 91 mg/L, range 10-760 (n = 114) | Large, persistent variability in both eras; no SBGG chemistry yet. |
| Thermal end-member chloride | White 820 mg/L; Nehring about 700; CPI reservoir 739 | Reconstructed parent fluid 657-672 mg/L; 2024 outlet samples 740-860 mg/L | Modern values sit in the historical range. |
| Cl/B in thermal water | About 18 (White; Collar below Rhodes Road); nonthermal 40-60 | Sorey and Colvard 19.3 (1990-91); this project 20-22 | Stable to within a few percent over seven decades. |
| Barometric efficiency | Spring 6: 42 percent (r = 0.79); spring 12: 45 percent (r = 0.44); White's low-terrace vent 31n: 60-75 percent | STMGID MW3 and MW10: 0.29-0.34 (differenced) and 0.58-0.60 (level) | Different wells; a spring-vent value at the Lower Sinter Terrace has not been measured. |
| Water-level change at monitored wells | Springs up to 17 ft; strat wells 2, 5, 9: 14-26 ft; GS-1: 2.5 ft; Steinhardt: 7 ft with chloride 300 to 143 mg/L | 2025: Herz Domestic and NDOT declining about 0.2-0.3 ft/month; Herz Domestic tracks STMGID MW3 (r = 0.94) | Shared seasonal signal with the regional well plus a faster local decline, as in 1988-89. |

| Seismicity | White: responses to M5-class nearby events; Collar: M3.9 (1986) had no effect | 2021-26 catalog: four M3.0-3.5 events within 6 km in Jan-Mar 2024 | No consistent water-level step at STMGID wells; a lead only. |
