: Recent and older values side by side, with the comparability limit of each. {#tbl-oldnew}

The chloride comparison at the two logger reaches (@fig-collarcl) is the
clearest case. At Rhodes Road, Collar's two S10 values fall inside the NDEP
record, and this project's 2026 SBRR sample does too, so the upstream control
is chemically the same place it was in 1988-89. At Geiger Grade the NDEP
record is far more variable, from 10 to 760 mg/L, and Collar's three S70
values (130-418 mg/L) sit inside that scatter; because S70 carried only
0.1-3.7 cfs it may be a thermal side channel rather than the main creek, so
this match is provisional until Plate 4 is georeferenced. The discharge
comparison (@fig-discharge) needs more care than the chloride one. White's
1955 total of 1,125 gpm includes about 315 gpm from wells and is not
comparable with the creek-inflow values; only creek-inflow rows are plotted on
one axis, and Shump's value, made with specific conductivity, is labeled as
such. Applying this project's two-station flux difference to Collar's own
cleanest survey (S10 against S77, 4 March 1989) gives about 32 L/s (508
gpm), against his reach-summed 660 gpm (42 L/s) for the same date, so the
two-station method probably reads about a quarter low in a survey like that.
The 58.7 L/s database value and the 27 L/s poster value should be read with
that in mind.

```{r fig-collarcl}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/collar_creek_chloride_comparison.png",
  "Steamboat Creek chloride at the Rhodes Road and Geiger Grade reaches: Collar's 1988-89 stations S10 and S70 (S70 provisional) against NDEP samples and this project's 2026 SBRR sample.",
  alt = "Two-panel scatter plot of chloride through time, 1988 to 2026, for the Rhodes Road and Geiger Grade reaches, showing Collar's stations, NDEP samples, and this project's sample.",
  id = "fig-collarcl",
  width = "85%"
)
```

Collar's spa-well observation also offers a test that can be run on current
data. If an intermittently pumped well near the low terrace produces a
weekday-weekend cycle in nearby heads, the resort-tank well (SBW_0002), which
is pumped intermittently by an air-lift, might leave a trace in the nearby
loggers. A weekday-weekend and seven-day spectral test on the daily mean
temperature of seven loggers (six terrace sites and SBRR, 83-98 days each, after removing a
15-day running mean) found none: weekend-minus-weekday differences were
within 0.9 C (the largest at the fissure logger), and no Kruskal-Wallis
test across weekdays had p below 0.7. Temperature is a weaker indicator than
the water levels Collar used, so this is a negative result for temperature
only; a pressure transducer in GS-1 or the resort-tank well would be the
direct equivalent.

## PHREEQC workflow: sample eligibility, databases, and interpretation

Aqueous speciation and saturation-index modeling is run through the real
PHREEQC 3 executable [@phreeqc] (the standalone program itself, not an R
reimplementation) against every sample with complete enough chemistry to
support it (312 real samples as of this writing), with a thermodynamic
database auto-selected per sample by temperature and total dissolved solids
and a documented fallback when the first choice fails to converge, as
described in the Background section above. What follows is the actual
workflow behind that number: which samples get modeled, how their chemistry
is assembled and cleaned up before PHREEQC ever sees it, and what the
output is actually used to decide.

**Sample eligibility.** Not every sample in the database gets run through
PHREEQC. A sample qualifies once it has pH, temperature, and major-ion
concentrations for chloride, sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, and
alkalinity: the minimum set a real speciation calculation needs, not just
whatever happens to be on hand. Field-measured pH and temperature are
preferred over laboratory-reported values when both exist, since a lab
reading taken days after collection has already drifted from in-situ
conditions; lab values are used only when no field measurement exists.
Additional analytes (silica, sulfate, lithium, boron, and a handful of
trace metals) are pulled in when available but aren't themselves
gatekeeping. Samples that don't clear this bar aren't silently dropped,
either: each is logged with the specific field it's missing, so the real,
and currently still substantial, gap between how many samples exist and how
many are PHREEQC-ready stays visible instead of disappearing into an
unexplained smaller number.

**Assembling and cleaning the chemistry first.** Samples come from several
sources spanning more than seventy years (field sampling, NDEP's routine
and public-records-request chemistry, and historical literature (Sorey and
Colvard, Mariner and Janik, and Skalbeck) transcribed directly rather than
merely cited) and those sources don't agree on units or on how alkalinity
is reported. Every concentration is standardized to mg/L before it reaches
a SOLUTION block, and any alkalinity value reported on a CaCO3 basis is
converted to this project's standard HCO3-mass-equivalent basis using the
real 50.05/61.02 equivalent-weight ratio (a conversion factor of 1.2189).
Getting this right turned out to matter more than it sounds like it should:
an earlier version of this pipeline simply left alkalinity out for one
major chemistry source, which alone pushed median charge-balance error
from a real ~0.7% up to a misleadingly bad ~60% for the exact same samples:
a data-handling artifact, not an actual analytical problem, and a good
reminder to check a "bad" charge balance before assuming the chemistry
itself is at fault.

**End-member grouping.** Samples with complete chemistry are assigned to
one of three groups (a thermal end-member (outlet and thermal-well
samples), mixed waters (chemistry carrying a partial but real thermal
signature), and dilute background waters) using the hydrochemical-facies
clustering described in the next section, cross-checked against PHREEQC's
own fluid-type classification rather than just asserted from the site-type
label on file. This is what makes the conservative-tracer check below, and
the Cl/B comparison in the preliminary results section, real
chemically-defined groups rather than an arbitrary site-based split.

**Conservative-tracer evaluation.** Four ratios (Cl/B, Na/Cl, Li/Cl, and
SiO2/Cl) are tracked across every era of chemistry on file (the 1950s, the
1990s, and the present) specifically to ask whether the real thermal
end-member's composition has stayed stable over seven decades, independent
of whatever a chloride-conductance calibration eventually finds. A ratio
that drifts meaningfully through time, or differs systematically between
eras constitutes real evidence about source-fluid stability (see the
preliminary Cl/B result in @fig-clb below) rather than folded quietly into
one pooled average that would hide exactly that question.

**Mixing and inverse modeling.** A two-end-member conservative-mixing
fraction is computed directly from chloride, then used to build a real
PHREEQC `MIX` block combining the two end-member solutions at that fraction
and comparing PHREEQC's own predicted speciation against the sample's
observed chemistry: a genuine test of the mixing hypothesis, not just an
arithmetic ratio. `INVERSE_MODELING` goes further, solving for mixing
fractions and mineral mass transfer simultaneously, within stated elemental
uncertainty bounds. One mixing run and two real inverse-modeling runs exist
as of this writing, and both inverse runs now report zero feasible models
(a correction from earlier text in this project: a parser bug (fixed
2026-10-25) had been reading PHREEQC's own echoed-back input-solution
composition as if it were a found solution, reporting a false "1 candidate
solution" for the first real inverse run (target: Soccer Field Monitoring
Well, end-members: sample 816/829) when PHREEQC's own raw output in fact
says "Number of models found: 0." That first run uses a representative (not
time-paired) thermal/meteoric end-member pair, because no two chloride
samples have yet been collected close enough together in time to serve as a
genuinely paired end-member set) exactly the gap the calibration sampling
plan above is meant to close. A second, gas-informed inverse run, described
in the Results section below, uses a reconstructed deep parent-fluid
composition as the thermal end-member and also finds zero feasible
solutions, traced to real post-mortem residuals (on Alkalinity, C(4), Ca,
and K) exceeding the stated uncertainty bound: a genuine infeasibility, not
a numerical-plumbing artifact this time. The automated parser's own
remaining gap (it has never correctly extracted a solution's
mineral-mass-transfer numbers from PHREEQC's raw text output) is now moot
for both of this project's real runs, since neither found a feasible
solution for it to extract from.

**Forward reaction-path titration.** Given that real inverse-modeling
attempts against the Lower Sinter Terrace flowpath consistently find zero
feasible solutions, a complementary forward method was built: mix two named
end-members at a known (stored or freshly computed) conservative fraction
with a PHREEQC `MIX` block, then use a PHREEQC `REACTION` block to
explicitly step one or more candidate mineral phases' mass transfer, in
both directions (net precipitation and net dissolution), and compare the
resulting modeled trajectory against the target sample's own real chemistry
at each step. The method was also used to test two concrete hypotheses
against SBS_0001, whose own chemistry (the highest sulfate and lowest
alkalinity of its peer group) pointed toward a non-carbonate explanation:
adding sulfate or fluoride mineral phases as additional candidates, and
substituting a different, higher-sulfate meteoric end-member in place of
the standard one. Full results are reported below.

**Assumptions and limitations of the forward titration method.** Four are
stated here plainly, since they bear directly on how much weight the
results below can carry. First, every candidate phase supplied to a given
run is titrated by the identical reaction-progress amount at each step:
there is no constraint, chemical or otherwise, that the system actually
dissolves or precipitates two phases in a one-to-one ratio; a result is
only as good as that simplifying choice. Second, a single mixing fraction
is held fixed for the whole titration, computed once from chloride before
the reaction is explored: the two are not jointly fit, so a real sample
whose best explanation actually involves *both* a different mixing fraction
and reaction could be mis-scored under this method. Third, the fit metric
compares PHREEQC's modeled values directly against reported lab
concentrations with no allowance for analytical uncertainty; a sample
within ordinary analytical error of the model looks exactly as "wrong" as
one with a real, geologically meaningful discrepancy. Fourth, and
demonstrated concretely rather than just asserted, results are conditional
on which candidate phases are supplied at all: the sensitivity test run
against SBS_0001, below, shows the same target's best-fit error ranging
from 44.5 percent down to 30.6 percent depending on phase and end-member
choices alone, with no single choice fully resolving the underlying
tension. SBRR's own status as a conservative, not theoretically pure,
meteoric reference (stated above) compounds all four points, since every
one of these tests inherits that same starting assumption.

**Interpretation framework.** Every PHREEQC run in this project is
ultimately answering one of three questions, not run just because the
chemistry happened to be complete enough to try: are the real water
types here chemically distinct from each other, is conductance
behaving conservatively enough to stand in for chloride, and has the
thermal end-member's own composition held up over the full
seventy-year record. A modeling result that doesn't actually bear on
one of those three questions isn't reported here just because it's
available.

**Chloride-to-boron ratio across seven decades.** A two-sample comparison
of the curated thermal end-member (seven historical samples from Sorey and
Colvard [@sorey1992]; six modern samples from this project's own field
campaign) finds the ratio is similar in magnitude but not statistically
identical: 19.6 for 1950-1991 versus 21.9 for 2024-2026 (t = -2.92, 9.9
degrees of freedom, p = 0.015), shown in @fig-clb. This is real evidence
against a wholesale change in source water, alongside a small, real shift
whose cause (an analytical-method difference between eras, versus a genuine
geochemical change of roughly 12%) remains an open question this proposal's
work is designed to resolve further.

```{r fig-clb}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/cl_b_ratio_by_era.png",
  "Chloride-to-boron ratio in real thermal end-member samples, 1950-2026.",
  alt = "Scatter plot of chloride-to-boron ratio by well name, comparing 1950-1991 samples to 2024-2026 samples.",
  id = "fig-clb"
)
```

**Geothermometer divergence.** Sodium/potassium and quartz/chalcedony
geothermometers, applied to the same real thermal samples, diverge
systematically: quartz sits below measured discharge temperature,
sodium/potassium sits above it, exactly as expected for a single
cooling, diluting flow path from a genuinely hot (roughly
150-250 degree Celsius) reservoir rather than two disconnected water
types, as shown in @fig-geo.

```{r fig-geo}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/geothermometer_comparison.png",
  "Geothermometer estimates versus measured discharge temperature, per-well mean across all real thermal samples with complete chemistry.",
  alt = "Paired-point plot comparing sodium/potassium and quartz/chalcedony geothermometer temperature estimates to measured discharge temperature, per well.",
  id = "fig-geo"
)
```

**Are these samples equilibrated enough to trust Na/K at face value?**
Every Na/K reservoir-temperature estimate already reported in this proposal
assumes the sampled fluid has reacted long enough with its host rock to
approach chemical equilibrium: an assumption that has not, until now, been
tested directly. A Giggenbach (1988) Na-K-square-root-Mg ternary, built
from the same real PHREEQC-conditioned chemistry for all seven flowpath
samples, answers this directly, shown in @fig-giggenbach: the fissure and
resort tank plot inside the Full Equilibrium field, the three real springs
and seep sit in the Partial Equilibrium band, SBW_0001 sits just into the
Immature field, and SBRR (the dilute meteoric reference) plots at the
magnesium-rich corner, exactly where a cold, unreacted water should. This
is independent support for trusting the Na/K estimates already used
throughout this proposal for the fissure, resort tank, and the three
springs, and a specific, real caution that SBW_0001's own Na/K estimate is
the least chemically mature of the group.

```{r fig-giggenbach}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/giggenbach_ternary.png",
  "Giggenbach (1988) Na-K-sqrt(Mg) maturity ternary, real PHREEQC-conditioned chemistry, all seven flowpath samples.",
  alt = "Ternary diagram with Na, K, and square-root-Mg vertices, showing seven labeled points relative to Full Equilibrium, Partial Equilibrium, and Immature Waters fields.",
  id = "fig-giggenbach"
)
```

**A second, independent water-type check.** A Cl-SO4-HCO3 ternary
(Giggenbach 1991), shown in @fig-anionternary, cross-checks the Piper
diagram's own water-type read with a different classification scheme: all
six real thermal samples fall inside the Mature Waters field, and SBRR
falls inside Peripheral Waters near the bicarbonate corner: agreeing with,
not contradicting, the Piper diagram's own separation of SBRR from the
thermal cluster.

```{r fig-anionternary}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/anion_ternary.png",
  "Cl-SO4-HCO3 ternary (Giggenbach 1991), real PHREEQC-conditioned chemistry, all seven flowpath samples.",
  alt = "Ternary diagram with chloride, sulfate, and bicarbonate vertices, showing seven labeled points relative to Mature Waters, Steam-heated, and Peripheral Waters fields.",
  id = "fig-anionternary"
)
```

**Does a genuine multicomponent equilibrium exist, or only the
quartz/chalcedony pair already reported?** The quartz-versus-Na/K
divergence already described above only ever compares two minerals at a
time. The test for a shared equilibration temperature (Reed and Spycher
1980) is whether several candidate minerals' saturation indices cross zero
at approximately the same temperature at once, using the full real 25-300
degree Celsius, 13-step temperature sweep already stored in
`PHREEQC_Temp_Sweep` for all six real thermal samples: no new PHREEQC
execution was needed to check this. The honest answer, shown in
@fig-mineraleq, is that it does not: quartz and chalcedony cross zero
within roughly 15-50 degrees Celsius of each sample's own measured
discharge temperature, but calcite and dolomite stay supersaturated across
almost the entire explored range, and anhydrite and fluorite stay
undersaturated throughout. At no real sample do two or more minerals
besides the quartz/chalcedony pair itself converge within 15 degrees
Celsius of one another (confirmed directly, not assumed, for every sample
in @tbl-geotherm). This does not undermine the quartz-versus-Na/K story
already told throughout this proposal; it sharpens it, by confirming that
quartz/chalcedony's own apparent agreement is real and not an artifact of
only checking two minerals while ignoring others that might have told a
different story.

```{r fig-mineraleq}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/mineral_equilibration.png",
  "Multicomponent mineral-equilibration diagram: saturation index vs. temperature for six candidate minerals at the six thermal samples plus SBBV (downstream creek, not itself thermal), from the stored PHREEQC_Temp_Sweep output.",
  alt = "Six-panel faceted line plot of saturation index versus temperature for calcite, dolomite, quartz, chalcedony, anhydrite, and fluorite, one panel per real thermal sample, with a dashed vertical line at each sample's measured discharge temperature.",
  id = "fig-mineraleq"
)
```

```{r tbl-geotherm}
geo_tbl <- read.csv("data/derived/phreeqc/geothermometer_summary_table.csv")
geo_tbl$multicomponent_converges <- ifelse(geo_tbl$multicomponent_converges, "Yes", "No")
knitr::kable(
  geo_tbl[, c("location_name", "measured_temp_c", "T_NaK_gigg_C", "T_NaK_four_C",
              "T_quartz_C", "T_chalcedony_C", "multicomponent_converges")],
  digits = 1, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Sample", "Measured T (C)", "Na/K (Giggenbach)", "Na/K (Fournier)",
                "Quartz", "Chalcedony", "2+ minerals converge?"),
  caption = "Geothermometer comparison, all eight flowpath samples including the downstream creek station SBBV, sorted by measured discharge temperature. The Na/K estimates at SBRR (256 C) and SBBV (197 C) are shown for completeness but are not physically meaningful at these dilute, non-thermal creek sites, consistent with the caveat stated elsewhere in this proposal. No sample shows two or more minerals besides quartz/chalcedony converging within 15 C of each other."
)
```

Including SBBV extends the picture one step downstream. Its quartz (64 C)
and chalcedony (45 C) equilibration temperatures sit between SBRR's (52 C
and 36 C) and the thermal features', while its measured temperature (23.7
C) is only about 8 C above SBRR's (15.2 C). Silica at SBBV therefore still
carries a faint thermal signature, in the same direction as its elevated
chloride, even though no mineral set converges on a shared equilibration
temperature there either (@fig-mineraleq). Its Na/K estimate, like
SBRR's, reflects dilute water and is not interpreted as a reservoir
temperature.

## Fissure gas geochemistry: a new, independent dataset

In April 2026, T. Fischer and K. Mtili (UCSB) collected three real free-gas
samples at the Lower Sinter Terrace fissure and an adjacent degassing area
across the road, with P. Ruprecht: dry-gas composition and carbon isotopes
analyzed at Fischer's Volatiles Lab (UCSB), noble-gas ratios at P. Barry's
lab (WHOI). This is the first gas-chemistry dataset this project has access
to, and the only Steamboat-specific gas chemistry on file anywhere besides
Mariner and Janik's [-@mariner1995] 1991-1994 well-23-5 analyses. One
sample (NV26-2) carries a flagged contamination risk (the field team noted
a possible Giggenbach-bottle leak, and it was also collected where sampling
broke through fresh asphalt that the gas was visibly escaping through) and
is treated accordingly below, not silently averaged in with the other two.

Because near-surface vent gas is never air-free, every sample is first
corrected for atmospheric entrainment using the standard assumption
that measured O2 is entirely atmospheric: air-derived N2 is estimated
from the dry-air N2/O2 ratio (3.773) and subtracted before the
remaining species are renormalized. This correction, not a new method
invented for this project, is applied before the D'Amore and Panichi
[-@damore1980] multicomponent gas geothermometer (the same
implementation already used and literature-validated in the Background
section) is run on each corrected composition.

**A first, independent gas-chemistry check.** The three real April 2026
fissure gas samples described in the Methods section give a second,
independent line of evidence on reservoir temperature and fluid stability.
Air-corrected gas ratios (CO2/N2, H2S/CO2, N2/Ar, CH4/CO2) for the two
unflagged samples (NV26-1, NV26-3) fall within, or close to, the range
Mariner and Janik [-@mariner1995] report for well 23-5 three decades
earlier, shown in @fig-gascomp; NV26-2's ratios sit well outside that
range, consistent with its flagged contamination. D'Amore-Panichi
gas-geothermometer estimates for NV26-1 and NV26-3 (228 and 181 degrees
Celsius) bracket Mariner and Janik's own well-23-5 T-DP range (173-200
degrees Celsius), shown in @fig-gastherm, while the gas-estimated
temperatures for all three real samples sit well above their own measured
vent temperatures (96-99.5 degrees Celsius): the same
cooling-diluting-flow-path pattern already seen in the water
geothermometers above, now independently reproduced by gas chemistry.
NV26-1 is co-located with SBF_0001, a real water sample collected May 1,
2026 with its own complete major-ion and stable-isotope chemistry (chloride
815 mg/L, delta-18-O -12.3 per mil, delta-D -114 per mil): the first point
in this project with both gas and water chemistry from the same location, a
pairing Chapter 4's mixing-model work is specifically positioned to use
going forward.

```{r fig-gascomp}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/gas_composition_comparison.png",
  "Air-corrected fissure gas ratios (NV26-1/2/3, April 2026) versus Mariner and Janik's (1995) well 23-5.",
  alt = "Faceted scatter plot comparing four gas composition ratios between the new fissure gas samples and historical well 23-5 values.",
  id = "fig-gascomp"
)
```

```{r fig-gastherm}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/gas_geothermometry_comparison.png",
  "D'Amore-Panichi gas-geothermometer estimates versus measured field temperature for the three real fissure gas samples.",
  alt = "Point plot comparing gas-geothermometer temperature estimates to measured field temperature for three fissure gas samples, with the historical well 23-5 range shown as reference lines.",
  id = "fig-gastherm"
)
```

## A gas-informed parent-fluid reconstruction and flowpath trace

NV26-1's gas composition is paired with sample 816 (SBF_0001, the
fissure water sample), the only real water-gas pair this project has.
A first-pass, explicitly simplified reconstruction works backward from
each measured (post-boiling) fluid toward its likely pre-boiling
"parent" composition, then traces both the parent and the measured
fluid forward through the system to the downstream creek:

1. **Reservoir temperature.** The Giggenbach sodium/potassium
   geothermometer (not quartz/chalcedony, which this project's own data
   consistently places *below* measured discharge temperature at
   Steamboat; see the geothermometer-divergence result above) is used as
   the reservoir temperature, since it comes out above measured
   temperature here, as expected for a cooling, diluting flow path.
2. **Steam-loss fraction.** A standard single-step adiabatic
   enthalpy-balance calculation (saturated-liquid/-vapor enthalpies from a
   steam-table lookup) gives the fraction of the parent fluid's mass lost
   to steam between the reservoir temperature and the measured discharge
   temperature.
3. **Conservative species.** Chloride, sodium, potassium, sulfate, boron,
   lithium, bromide, fluoride, strontium, and alkalinity are scaled back
   by (1 - steam-loss fraction): boiling concentrates the residual liquid,
   so the parent values are lower than measured, not higher.
4. **Gas add-back.** NV26-1's air-corrected carbon dioxide-to-hydrogen
   sulfide ratio is used to seed a PHREEQC `GAS_PHASE` equilibration at
   the reservoir's own saturation pressure (several atmospheres, not 1
   atmosphere), re-setting pH and carbonate speciation to a plausible
   pre-boiling state.

This whole method is a first pass built to be refined, not a finished
geothermometric technique: it assumes single-step (not continuous) boiling
and that carbon dioxide/hydrogen sulfide partition essentially completely
into the escaping vapor, and it applies the one real gas sample (NV26-1) to
both the fissure and the resort-tank water samples, since no gas sample
exists at the resort tank itself.

**What well actually feeds the resort tank, and what does its history
say?** The fissure well (SBF_0001) itself has no `Wells` record at all in
this project's database: its total depth, casing, and completion interval
are genuinely unknown, not just unrecorded by oversight. What stands in for
that missing construction record is the fissure's own temperature-logger
behavior at the eruption site itself (the inverse correlation between
paired loggers already cited as poster-stage evidence) and the gas
chemistry's own reservoir-temperature read (the D'Amore-Panichi estimate
above), neither of which needs a known well depth to be informative, but
neither of which can substitute for one either. The resort tank's own well
is better constrained, though not confirmed: a real NBMG `Geothermal_Wells`
proximity check finds SBW_0002 sitting within 10-24 meters of three named
historic wells: Carver Geothermal Well (8.6 meters deep), and two wells
explicitly operated by Steamboat Resort itself, Steamboat No. 2 (36.6
meters, roughly 120 feet) and Steamboat No. 4 (68.6 meters, roughly 225
feet), both listed as abandoned production wells. Steamboat No. 4 is very
plausibly the same well White [-@white1968c] describes as erupting
continuously once drilling intersected its aquifer in 1947-48 (Chapter 2's
background on the Low Terrace): a real historical precedent for an
uncontrolled discharge at essentially this same spot, decades before the
resort tank's current air-lift pump was installed. This places the resort
tank's own history inside the field's broader operational arc: a
resort-operated production well predating Ormat's and SB Geo's later,
field-wide development [@dhakal2025] (Chapter 1), now repurposed as a
pumped outflow tap rather than a free-flowing or company-operated
production well. Framed this way, the resort tank is best read as a deep
fluid source whose chemistry is measurably altered by the act of extraction
itself (the air-lift pump's forced aeration), not as a naturally
discharging point comparable to the fissure or the real springs: a
distinction already built into how this proposal treats its chemistry
throughout (as-measured, as-pumped, never reconstructed as a free-flowing
parent fluid). Three candidate wells sitting within 24 meters of each other
is too close to confidently pick one without more information, so this
remains a real, named lead, not a confirmed well identity.

**A limitation specific to the resort-tank sample.** The well feeding the
resort tank is pumped with a true air-lift pump, confirmed by its
intermittent discharge pattern: compressed air is injected into the well to
lift the water, rather than the water flowing or flashing naturally. That
is a fundamentally different degassing pathway from the fissure's natural
adiabatic boiling that this method's steam-loss correction assumes, and it
is a more parsimonious explanation for the resort tank's own behavior than
the method's own physics: forced, intermittent contact with injected air
plausibly strips carbon dioxide (and may add oxygen) regardless of how
much, if any, the deep fluid itself boiled on the way up, which would
explain both the resort tank's unusually high measured field pH and the
gas-equilibration convergence failure reported below without invoking any
property of the deep reservoir fluid at all. The resort tank's own "parent
fluid" reconstruction is still computed and reported below, for
completeness and because the exercise is instructive about the method's
limits, but it should not be read as a reliable estimate of the deep
reservoir fluid at the resort well: its as-measured (as-pumped) chemistry
is used instead everywhere it appears as a target or end-member elsewhere
in this proposal (the reaction-path titration and inverse-modeling sections
below). Every PHREEQC run in this reconstruction uses the LLNL
thermodynamic database (automatically recommended for every sample here,
since all are geothermal-temperature fluids), explicitly logged (along with
each input sample's own charge-balance error and each gas-equilibration
step's convergence status) to
`data/derived/phreeqc/parent_fluid_diagnostics.csv`, so a real convergence
failure is reported, not hidden (see Results).

The reconstructed parent fluid, the as-measured fissure and resort-tank
fluids, a nearby Lower Sinter Terrace well (SBW_0001), and this project's
two Steamboat Creek chloride-mass-balance stations (SBRR, near-field; SBBV,
downstream: the same two stations `chloride_mass_balance.R` already uses)
are assembled into one real flowpath table and figure, tracking chloride,
sodium, sulfate, silica, boron, pH, calcite and quartz saturation indices,
sodium/potassium and quartz geothermometer estimates, and
delta-18-O/delta-2-H across every node with real data. A small,
honestly-scoped statistical check (three real thermal points: fissure,
resort tank, and the nearby well) asks whether their independently derived
sodium/potassium reservoir-temperature estimates are consistent with one
shared parent fluid.

**What this section covers, in sequence.**

This subsection covers one connected analysis built across several steps,
in this order: (1) a steam-loss and gas-add-back correction reconstructs
the fissure's deep "parent fluid" using the one available real fissure gas
sample; (2) the identical method is also applied, diagnostically, to the
resort tank, but the well feeding the resort tank is pumped with a true,
intermittent air-lift pump, a mechanically forced aeration process the
method's own steam-loss physics does not represent, so the resulting
"agreement" between the two reconstructions is reported but not relied on
as evidence; (3) a six-database sensitivity sweep is run on the resort-tank
reconstruction because its gas-equilibration step failed to converge on
this project's default database; (4) that divergence is root-caused to the
resort tank's own high measured starting pH (9.0 versus the fissure's 8.3),
itself very plausibly a direct consequence of the air-lift pump's forced
aeration, not database choice, gas-load size, or a property of the deep
reservoir fluid; (5) the fissure's reconstructed parent fluid (not the
resort tank's) is then used as an end-member in real PHREEQC inverse
modeling against both targets, which finds zero feasible solutions,
attributed to a known PHREEQC numerical quirk, not a geochemical rejection
of the end-member; and (6) the reconstructed fissure parent fluid and the
as-measured chemistry at every other node, including the resort tank's own
as-pumped composition, are traced along a full flowpath from parent fluid
to the downstream creek. Each step is reported with its own real result
below.

**A gas-informed parent-fluid reconstruction.** Applying the method above
to sample 816 (the fissure) gives a steam-loss fraction of 19.4 percent
(reservoir 173.4 degrees Celsius, measured discharge 67.0 degrees Celsius),
a reconstructed parent chloride of 657 mg/L (below the measured 815 mg/L,
as boiling concentrates the residual liquid), and (once the reconstructed
fluid is re-equilibrated with NV26-1's real gas composition at reservoir
pressure (8.7 atmospheres)) a substantially more acidic parent pH (5.5,
versus 8.3 measured) and calcite/dolomite saturation indices that flip from
mildly supersaturated to clearly undersaturated. This is the expected
direction for a deep, gas-charged fluid that has not yet degassed:
carbonate scaling is a surface/shallow phenomenon as carbon dioxide escapes
and pH rises, not a deep-reservoir one, shown in @fig-parentfluid. Applying
the identical method to the resort-tank sample (815) gives a similar
steam-loss fraction (20.8 percent) and a parent chloride within 2.3 percent
of the fissure's own reconstructed parent (657 vs. 672 mg/L): closer than
the two samples' raw measured values (815 vs. 849 mg/L). This agreement is
reported, not relied upon: the resort-tank well is pumped with a true,
intermittent air-lift pump, a forced-aeration process this method's
steam-loss physics does not represent, so its reconstructed "parent" is not
a trustworthy estimate of a deep fluid, and the tight Cl agreement could
just as easily be a coincidence of applying an inapplicable correction as
it could be real evidence of a shared source. Potassium, sulfate, lithium,
and strontium converge less tightly (9-15 percent apart even after
correction), which could reflect either minor water-rock reaction
differences along slightly different flow paths, real sampling/analytical
variability, or the resort tank's pumping artifact: not resolved further
here. The resort-tank sample's own gas-equilibration step did not converge
(a PHREEQC limitation at this fluid's measured pH of 9.0 combined with the
imposed acid-gas load, logged to `parent_fluid_diagnostics.csv` rather than
hidden), so its reconstructed parent pH and saturation indices are not
reported: only its conservative-species concentrations, which do not depend
on that step.

**A note on the field-temperature correction.** A field-temperature unit
bug (the project's Fluke field thermometer reports Fahrenheit, mislabeled
as Celsius downstream of ingestion) was found and fixed after these
reconstructions were first run, and every number above reflects the
corrected temperatures. The steam-loss fractions and reconstructed parent
chloride changed materially (the fissure's steam-loss fraction moved from
an originally-miscalculated 4.2 percent to the corrected 19.4 percent, for
example), but the qualitative conclusion (the two independently
reconstructed parent fluids converge more tightly than the raw measured
values do) holds under both the original and corrected temperatures.

```{r fig-parentfluid}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/parent_fluid_comparison.png",
  "A. Measured versus gas-informed reconstructed parent-fluid composition for the fissure sample. B. The resulting conservative-chloride thermal mixing fraction for three real Lower Sinter Terrace samples, computed with the measured fluid versus the reconstructed parent fluid as the thermal end-member.",
  alt = "Two-panel figure: bar chart comparing measured and parent-fluid concentrations of ten conservative species; point plot comparing mixing fractions under two end-member choices for three target samples.",
  id = "fig-parentfluid"
)
```


**Does the choice of thermodynamic database matter here, especially given
the resort-tank fluid's convergence failure?** No: a six-database
sensitivity sweep traced the resort tank's gas-equilibration convergence
failure to its own unusually high measured field pH (9.0 versus the
fissure's 8.3), not to database choice: forcing its starting pH down to
match the fissure's converges cleanly on every database tested and lands
within 0.1 pH units of the fissure's own result. That high starting pH most
plausibly reflects the resort well's own air-lift pump (above), not a
deep-fluid property. Full method and the figure are in notebook 06
(`notebooks/06_phreeqc_geochemical_modeling.qmd`), since this result feeds
the planned second manuscript, not the calibration thesis itself.

**Feeding the reconstructed parent fluid into real inverse modeling.**
Running this project's existing PHREEQC inverse-modeling framework
(end-members: the fissure's reconstructed parent fluid (not the resort
tank's, for the reasons given above) and the meteoric reference well;
candidate phases: calcite, quartz, chalcedony) against the two real target
samples with complete chemistry (SBW_0001, SBW_0002, both used as-measured)
finds zero feasible mixing-plus-mineral-transfer solutions for either
target. This is not read as a geochemical rejection of the parent-fluid
end-member: the raw PHREEQC output traces the failure to the same tiny (on
the order of 1e-9), numerically spurious residual on an unused trace redox
couple (chlorine or carbon oxidation states that play no real role in this
chemistry) already documented as a known PHREEQC execution-plumbing
limitation in this project's own synthetic self-tests. Reported plainly as
a current limitation of the inverse-modeling tool for this specific
end-member pairing, not silently retried until something "worked." A
separate, independent inverse-modeling attempt against SBW_0001 directly
(end-members: the fissure and SBRR rather than the reconstructed parent
fluid; candidate phases: calcite, dolomite), re-run after the
field-temperature correction, now finds a genuine feasible solution once
the analytical uncertainty is loosened to 12 percent or more: a materially
different and more informative result than the pre-fix search, which found
none at any uncertainty up to 15 percent. At the standard 5 percent
uncertainty the model is infeasible for several elements at once
(alkalinity, carbon, calcium, and potassium); at 10 and 11 percent a
single, cleanly shrinking calcium residual remains (2.5e-4 mol at 10
percent, 1.1e-4 mol at 11 percent); at 12 percent this residual clears and
PHREEQC reports one real feasible model: a 70.6/29.4 percent fissure/SBRR
mixture plus a net *dissolution* of 4.0e-4 mol calcite and 1.3e-4 mol
dolomite. At 15 percent uncertainty a second feasible solution is found
with a somewhat different mixture (65.8/34.2 percent) and similar net
dissolution. This is a real, quantitative point of agreement with the
forward titration result below: both methods independently converge on net
calcite-plus-dolomite *dissolution* on the order of a few times 1e-4 mol
along this flowpath, not precipitation. Read together, a feasible
two-end-member-plus-carbonate model for SBW_0001 exists, but only once the
uncertainty allowed on the underlying chemical analyses is relaxed beyond
this project's usual 5 percent default: consistent with real analytical
uncertainty on these samples' major-ion measurements being larger than
typically assumed, a genuine and testable hypothesis for a tighter future
sampling round rather than a modeling dead end.

**A forward alternative: titrating calcite and dolomite instead of asking
the solver to search for them.** Because the inverse search above is only
feasible at a loosened uncertainty tolerance, a complementary, better-posed
question is to run the reaction forward at the standard, un-loosened
analytical uncertainty: mix the fissure and SBRR at their real,
already-computed conservative mixing fraction, then explicitly step calcite
and dolomite mass transfer (both net precipitation and net dissolution) and
see what the resulting chemistry trajectory looks like, shown in
@fig-reactionpath. The result is a genuine interior optimum, not an edge
artifact of the explored range: a modest net *dissolution* of calcite and
dolomite (on the order of one-tenth of a millimole, 1.17e-4 mol combined)
brings the combined calcium, magnesium, and alkalinity error down from
roughly 45 to 48 percent at pure conservative mixing to about 23 percent at
the best fit. That is a substantial improvement over mixing alone, but it
does not fully reconcile the target: alkalinity in particular never reaches
its observed value anywhere in the titrated range. Chloride stays exactly
conservative across every step, confirming the titration moves only the
carbonate system, as intended. Read together, the inverse and forward
results now reinforce each other on both the sign and the rough magnitude
of the needed correction: net calcite-plus-dolomite dissolution, not
precipitation, order 1e-4 mol. The inverse search needs a looser
uncertainty tolerance to call this feasible in a strict least-squares
sense; the forward titration shows the same direction and size of
correction brings the fit most of the way there even without loosening
anything, with alkalinity as the one component that resists full
reconciliation either way: a genuine part of the answer, not a dead end,
and a concrete target for tighter future alkalinity measurements at this
specific well.

```{r fig-reactionpath}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/reaction_path_titration.png",
  "Forward PHREEQC REACTION-path titration of calcite and dolomite into the fissure+SBRR conservative mix, compared against SBW_0001's real observed Ca/Mg/Alkalinity (dashed lines) and the best-fit reaction progress (dotted line).",
  alt = "Five-panel figure: calcium, magnesium, alkalinity, calcite saturation index, and dolomite saturation index, each plotted against net reaction progress, with a dashed horizontal reference line for the real observed value and a dotted vertical line marking the best-fit reaction progress.",
  id = "fig-reactionpath"
)
```

**Running the same titration against the three real Low Sinter Terrace
springs tells a more complicated story than the saturation-index-only view
suggested.** The earlier forward-mixing figure, based only on calcite and
dolomite saturation index and pH, showed the three springs (SBS_0001,
SBS_0002, SBS_0003) sitting much closer to the pure-mixing curve than
SBW_0001. Running the identical forward titration against each spring
directly, using the full Ca/Mg/Alkalinity mass balance rather than
saturation index alone, does not fully confirm that picture, shown in
@fig-reactionpath-comparison. SBS_0002 needs almost no reaction correction
at all, consistent with the earlier read. SBS_0003 needs a small correction
and reaches a good fit (19.7 percent combined error, the best of the four
real targets). SBS_0001, however, shows the **worst** fit of all four
targets even after titration (44.5 percent), despite needing a
comparatively modest reaction-progress correction: its real calcium sits
well above anything the explored titration range can reach, while its real
alkalinity sits below the titration curve's own value at every explored
point, including the most negative (net-precipitation) step the real
Ca/Mg/alkalinity pool can physically support. These two demands pull in
opposite directions and cannot both be satisfied by this simple two-phase
model over a physically available range, not because the search was cut
short. Chloride stays exactly conservative at every step for every target,
so this is not an artifact of the conservative-tracer assumption itself.
SBW_0001 remains the target needing by far the largest correction and
showing the largest absolute improvement, but it is no longer the only
target this simple model struggles to explain: SBS_0001 does too, for a
different, specific reason.

```{r fig-reactionpath-comparison}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/reaction_path_fit_comparison.png",
  "Combined Ca/Mg/Alkalinity fit error at pure conservative mixing versus each target's own best-fit reaction progress, across all five real downgradient targets.",
  alt = "Dumbbell plot comparing fit error (percent) at pure mixing versus best-fit reaction progress for five samples: SBW_0001, SBW_0002, SBS_0001, SBS_0002, and SBS_0003.",
  id = "fig-reactionpath-comparison"
)
```

**A fifth real target: the resort tank (SBW_0002), run with a necessary
adjustment.** SBW_0002's own stored conservative mixing fraction against
the fissure and SBRR is 1.043, slightly above the valid 0 to 1 range: a
real, already-documented finding (this project's own earlier work), that
SBW_0002 is *more* concentrated than the fissure reference itself, not a
new problem. A fraction outside this range cannot be represented as a real
mixture of the two named end-members, so the fraction is clamped to 1.0
(pure fissure end-member, no meteoric dilution), before running the
titration, with the modeling implication stated explicitly rather than
silently worked around: the question being asked shifts from "does mixing
plus reaction explain this sample" to "does reaction alone, starting from
the pure thermal end-member, explain the small remaining gap." Under that
explicitly adjusted question, SBW_0002 fits extremely well: a combined
Ca/Mg/Alkalinity error of only 4.6 percent at a tiny net precipitation (on
the order of one-millionth of a mole), by far the best fit of any real
target tested on this flowpath, shown in @fig-reactionpath-comparison. This
titration uses SBW_0002's real as-measured (as-pumped) composition
throughout, not a reconstructed parent fluid, so the air-lift pump's effect
on gas chemistry and pH does not bear on it: calcium, magnesium, and
alkalinity are not the species an air-lift pump would be expected to alter,
so this excellent fit is read as a genuine, trustworthy result about how
closely SBW_0002's major-ion chemistry resembles the fissure's, independent
of the separate pH/gas-equilibration concerns raised above.

**Does a sulfate phase, or a different meteoric input, resolve SBS_0001's
own reaction-path tension?** SBS_0001's own chemistry (the highest sulfate,
lowest alkalinity of its peer group) suggested a non-carbonate explanation,
so seven real model variants (alternate mineral phases, alternate meteoric
end-members, and a combined variant) were tested against it directly. None
fully resolves the tension: the best result (30.6 percent combined error)
still falls short of SBS_0002's and SBS_0003's own baseline fits, and the
ranking of variants changes once a scoring bug affecting fluorite's own
fluoride prediction is fixed: a modest lesson in how sensitive this kind of
sensitivity test is to exactly what is scored. Full method, all seven
variants, and the figure are in notebook 06
(`notebooks/06_phreeqc_geochemical_modeling.qmd`), since this result feeds
the planned second manuscript, not the calibration thesis itself.

**Close on a map, far apart chemically.** SBS_0001 and SBW_0001 sit only
109 meters apart by their own real coordinates, shown in
@fig-proximity-map, yet behave about as differently as any two real
targets on this flowpath can: SBS_0001 is the worst-fitting target
tested (even after every sensitivity variant above), while SBW_0001
needs the largest reaction-progress correction of the original four
targets but also shows one of the largest real improvements once that
correction is applied. This is a concrete, mappable instance of the
principle already stated in this proposal's discussion of modeling
assumptions: physical proximity does not imply shared chemistry or a
shared flow path, and a defensible model has to be built from which
samples are genuinely chemically alike, not which ones happen to sit
close together.

```{r fig-proximity-map}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/lst_proximity_map.png",
  "Real lat/lon positions of the seven flowpath samples, with the five real downgradient targets colored and sized by their own best-fit reaction-path RMSE.",
  alt = "Map of seven points with latitude and longitude axes, two grey triangles for the fissure and SBRR reference end-members, and five colored circles for the real downgradient targets sized by fit error.",
  id = "fig-proximity-map"
)
```

**A real Piper diagram, independent of any PHREEQC modeling.** As a
direct, model-free check of the sulfate hypothesis above, a trilinear
Piper diagram was built from the same seven samples' real mg/L
chemistry converted to charge-equivalent percentages, shown in
@fig-piper. The honest result is a real, if slightly deflating,
negative one: SBS_0001 does not visibly separate from SBS_0002 or
SBS_0003 toward the anion triangle's sulfate corner. Chloride dominates
the anion budget so heavily in every real thermal sample on this
flowpath that SBS_0001's real, absolute sulfate excess (187 versus
63 to 167 milligrams per liter at the other targets) does not translate
into a large shift in charge-equivalent percentage terms. The diagram
still does real, useful work: it visually separates SBRR from the
thermal cluster exactly as expected, and groups the thermal samples
together on both the cation and anion triangles, a plain visual
confirmation of the facies picture already established statistically in
Chapter 4's hierarchical clustering and principal-components work.

```{r fig-piper}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/lst_piper_diagram.png",
  "Trilinear Piper diagram, built directly from real mg/L chemistry, for the fissure, SBRR, SBW_0001, SBW_0002, and the three real Low Sinter Terrace springs.",
  alt = "Standard Piper diagram with a cation triangle, an anion triangle, and a central diamond, with seven colored points for the seven real flowpath samples.",
  id = "fig-piper"
)
```

**Tracing the flowpath from parent fluid to the downstream creek.** Putting
the two reconstructed parent fluids, the as-measured fissure and
resort-tank chemistry, a nearby Lower Sinter Terrace well (SBW_0001), and
the two real Steamboat Creek chloride-mass-balance stations (SBRR, then
downstream SBBV) on one real flowpath, shown in @fig-evolution, gives a
coherent, data-supported picture: chloride, sodium, silica, and boron all
decline in the same order along the flowpath (parent/fissure/resort-tank
high, SBW_0001 roughly half, SBRR near background, SBBV measurably higher
than SBRR again): the same real chloride-flux difference between SBRR and
SBBV that already drives this project's own thermal-discharge estimate
(`chloride_mass_balance.R`), now shown constituent by constituent. pH rises
from the reconstructed parent (acidic) through the measured, partly
degassed discharge points (alkaline) to the creek (near-neutral to mildly
alkaline), consistent with progressive carbon dioxide loss. Calcite
saturation is undersaturated at the reconstructed parent, mildly
supersaturated at the two measured discharge points, and most
supersaturated at the nearby well and downstream creek: a real, specific
illustration of where calcite scaling risk is highest along this flow path.
The quartz geothermometer declines smoothly and plausibly along the same
sequence (118 and 99 degrees Celsius at the two warmest points, down to
53-62 degrees Celsius at the creek stations); the sodium/potassium
geothermometer does **not** behave this way at the two creek stations
(physically implausible values of 195-255 degrees Celsius), a known,
already-documented artifact of applying that geothermometer to dilute,
non-thermal water: shown for transparency, not as a real
reservoir-temperature estimate at those two points. Delta-18-O and
delta-2-H tell a complementary story: both creek stations sit close to each
other and more isotopically depleted than the fissure or resort-tank water,
consistent with the real thermal inflow being a small enough fraction of
total streamflow that it shifts the creek's conservative-tracer chemistry
(chloride) measurably while barely shifting its bulk isotopic signature,
which stays dominated by meteoric water.

```{r fig-evolution}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/fluid_evolution_flowpath.png",
  "Real chemistry, PHREEQC saturation indices, geothermometer estimates, and stable isotopes across the sampled Lower Sinter Terrace flowpath, from the two reconstructed parent fluids through measured discharge, a nearby well, and the two Steamboat Creek chloride-mass-balance stations.",
  alt = "Twelve-panel scatter plot showing chloride, sodium, sulfate, silica, boron, pH, calcite and quartz saturation indices, two geothermometer estimates, and two stable isotopes across seven real or reconstructed flowpath nodes.",
  id = "fig-evolution"
)
```

The three real, independently sampled thermal points (fissure, resort tank,
nearby well) give sodium/potassium reservoir-temperature estimates of
173.4, 179.2, and 180.2 degrees Celsius: a 6.8-degree range and a 2.1
percent coefficient of variation. Three points is too few for a formally
powered statistical test, stated plainly rather than dressed up with an
inappropriate p-value, but a spread this tight relative to the 50-100
degree Celsius divergence this project's own
geothermometer-vs-measured-temperature comparison already documents across
its full sample set is a real, specific piece of evidence consistent with
these three points sharing one deep source, not three independent ones.

**What the geothermometers say about hot and dissolving zones in the
shallow subsurface.** Reading the Na/K estimate, the quartz-equilibration
estimate, and the measured discharge temperature together for all six real
thermal features (not just the three used for the agreement test above)
turns the geothermometer divergence already documented in Chapter 2 into a
real diagnostic. At every single feature, quartz equilibration (99-127
degrees Celsius) sits above the measured discharge temperature, and Na/K
(173-190 degrees Celsius) sits higher still, in a real, three-stage cooling
signature: a shared deep reservoir around 175-190 degrees Celsius (Na/K,
slow to re-equilibrate), transit through a shallower zone still hot enough
to leave a quartz signature well above final discharge temperature, then a
last, near-surface step down to whatever temperature is actually measured
at the tap or pool. The SIZE of that last step is not uniform across
feature types, and it lines up with the gain/loss pattern below: the two
coolest real springs (SBS_0001, 47.8 degrees Celsius; SBS_0003, 39.6
degrees Celsius) show the largest gap between their quartz estimate and
their measured temperature (79 and 63 degrees Celsius respectively), while
the wells (SBW_0001, SBF_0001) show a smaller gap (28-51 degrees Celsius)
despite starting from a similar quartz-equilibration temperature. Read
together with the sulfate-gain/ alkalinity-loss pattern below, this is
consistent with the springs undergoing more near-surface processing (more
cooling, more atmosphere-driven chemical change) on the way to discharge
than the wells do, even though all of these features' deeper temperatures
agree closely. This does not identify a specific hot zone or dissolving
zone with a depth or a coordinate (that would need real well-log or
geophysical data this project does not yet have (Chapter 3)), but it does
say, with real numbers, that the shallow subsurface is not thermally or
chemically uniform between discharge points, and that springs and wells
experience that non-uniformity differently.

**The real thermal-infrared imagery itself.** The raster files behind this
project's previously qualitative-only description of the terrace's surface
thermal signature are now on file (resolving the gap previously flagged in
`docs/action_items_for_user.md`, item 12). The broad July 2025 drone
thermal-infrared survey, shown in @fig-tirbroad, overlays the full Lower
Sinter Terrace against satellite imagery, with labeled ground-control
points, a visible warm channel tracking Steamboat Creek, and the resort
well/pools area. A calibrated, zoomed-in thermal orthophoto of the fissure
area, shown in @fig-tirzoom, makes the two-discharge-style claim concrete
rather than only described in prose: discrete, bright point sources cluster
along the terrace's western margin (plausible active degassing/boiling
vents), while a broader, more diffuse warm signature tracks the creek
channel itself (more consistent with shallow seepage and mixing than
point-source degassing). This is still a qualitative, visual read, not a
digitized layer (turning either image into a real `Fault_Traces`-style
georeferenced layer (per this project's own established "ArcGIS out, ArcGIS
back in" workflow, already used for other literature figures) remains a
concrete next step, not yet done here), but it is now a real, visually
confirmed observation rather than one based on images shared informally.

**A first PHREEQC test using the gas data.** The gas isotope and
conservative-ratio data collected here are also a natural input to the
PHREEQC gas-phase modeling already described in the Background section,
for the first time a test was possible rather than only a synthetic
self-test: SBF_0001's real water chemistry was re-equilibrated against a
`GAS_PHASE` seeded with NV26-1's real, air-corrected CO2-to-H2S proportions
(96.5 to 3.5 percent) at 1 atmosphere, modeled as an open system
continuously resupplied by the fissure. Shown in @fig-gasphase, the result
is a real, substantive shift: pH drops from the water's measured 8.3 to a
modeled 5.7, and calcite, aragonite, and dolomite all move from
supersaturated (as this project's PHREEQC pipeline already finds for the
water alone) to undersaturated. Read plainly, this says the water as
sampled is not simply sitting in equilibrium with the vent gas as sampled:
either the two were not collected from truly the same fluid parcel, gas and
liquid separate before either is caught at the surface, or the real
reservoir pressure (not the 1 atmosphere used here as a simplification)
changes the picture. Any of those is a useful constraint on how this
system's gas and water should eventually be modeled together, not a result
to over-interpret from one sample pair.

```{r fig-gasphase}

  alt = "Bar chart comparing pH and three carbonate mineral saturation indices before and after equilibrating a real water sample with a real measured gas composition.",
  id = "fig-gasphase"
)
```

## A baseline chemical-evolution characterization of the flowpath

Everything in this subsection is read from the mixing, reaction-path, and
geothermometer runs already reported above: no new PHREEQC execution was
needed. The real samples feeding every result here were all collected
within the same field season, so this is explicitly a **one-time, same-era
baseline characterization**: a demonstration that this modeling approach
can reconstruct mixing, chemical evolution, and feature-type connectivity
along a real flowpath from a single snapshot of real data, not an iterative
refinement project. Further precision (tighter end-members, a real paired
uncertainty estimate for inverse modeling, resolving SBS_0001's own
unresolved tension) is explicitly deferred to the same-day synoptic
sampling round proposed in Chapter 5, not pursued further here.

This baseline does two things for the rest of the proposal. First, it
connects the fissure-specific geochemistry above directly to the
creek-scale conductivity-as-proxy work in Chapter 4: both are, at bottom,
asking how far, and in what chemical form, the same thermal signal travels
from its source, and the mixing fractions below are the quantitative link
between the two. Second, it gives a chemical baseline for the Lower Sinter
Terrace as it stood in this field season: after the June 2025 eruption,
following the two-year buildup described in Chapter 1, and while the
terrace is still visibly changing, including the new hot spring the author
and Dave found in August 2026 and the growing sulfur deposit documented the
following month. Every new feature found at the terrace from here forward
can be checked against this same mixing/gain-loss framework to ask the same
question asked of SBS_0001 and SBW_0001 below: does it share the fissure's
deep chemical signature, and if so, does it behave more like a well or more
like a spring once that water nears the surface? That is a concrete,
repeatable test this baseline makes available for the ongoing spring and
well remapping, not just a one-off result.

**How much of each discharge point is fissure-strength fluid, and how does
that connect to the downstream proxy record?** Using the real,
already-computed Cl-based mixing fraction against the fissure and SBRR
end-members, shown in @fig-mixingfraction, the three real Low Sinter
Terrace springs and seep sit at 0.77-0.89 (mostly fissure-strength fluid,
diluted only modestly), the nearby well (SBW_0001) sits lower at 0.57, and
the resort tank exceeds the fissure reference itself (1.04, already
documented as a finding, not an error). SBRR itself anchors the dilute end
by definition; its downstream partner SBBV, several kilometers further down
Steamboat Creek, still implies about 14 percent fissure-strength fluid by
chloride alone: the same signal, at a much smaller concentration, that
`chloride_mass_balance.R`'s own 58.7 liter-per-second thermal-discharge
estimate is built on. This is the direct link between the fissure-specific
chemistry above and the creek-scale conductivity-as-proxy work: the same
conservative mixing framework explains both.

```{r fig-mixingfraction}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/mixing_fraction_by_target.png",
  "Real Cl-based mixing fraction (fraction fissure end-member) for every real downgradient target, colored by feature type.",
  alt = "Horizontal bar chart of mixing fraction for six real targets, sorted from SBBV (lowest) to the resort tank (highest, exceeding 1).",
  id = "fig-mixingfraction"
)
```

```{r tbl-mixingfraction}
mix_tbl <- read.csv("data/derived/phreeqc/mixing_fraction_summary_table.csv")
knitr::kable(
  mix_tbl, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Target", "Feature type", "Mixing fraction (fissure end-member)"),
  caption = "Real Cl-based conservative-mixing fraction against the fissure (f=1) and SBRR (f=0) end-members, every real downgradient target, sorted low to high."
)
```

**What is gained or lost, species by species, and does it distinguish
feature types?** Comparing each real target's measured chemistry against
what the same Cl-based mixing fraction would predict if every species
traveled conservatively, shown in @fig-gainloss, sodium comes back
essentially conservative everywhere (within 6 percent), the direct
justification for treating chloride and sodium as reliable tracers in this
system. Potassium is modestly gained everywhere (13-31 percent), an open
signal plausibly reflecting mild clay or feldspar exchange, not chased
further here. Sulfate and alkalinity are where the real feature-type
distinction shows up, sharpened in @fig-springswells: **every spring and
the seep gain far more sulfate relative to conservative mixing than either
well** (44-62 percent versus -3 to 20 percent), and alkalinity is **gained
at both wells but lost at two of the three springs**: opposite signs for
the same species, split cleanly along feature type. Plausible mechanisms
for both: open spring and seep discharge points are exposed to the
atmosphere in a way a cased well is not, so near-surface oxidation of
residual hydrogen sulfide to sulfate, and carbon dioxide degassing that
would otherwise support alkalinity, both have more opportunity to happen
before a sample is ever collected.

```{r fig-gainloss}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/species_gainloss_heatmap.png",
  "Real measured concentration versus the conservative-mixing prediction for six species, for every real downgradient target, expressed as percent gained or lost.",
  alt = "Tile plot with targets on rows and species on columns, colored and labeled by percent deviation from conservative mixing.",
  id = "fig-gainloss"
)
```

```{r fig-springswells}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/springs_vs_wells_residuals.png",
  "Sulfate and alkalinity gain/loss relative to conservative mixing, grouped by feature type, isolating the clearest feature-type pattern from the full heatmap above.",
  alt = "Two-panel bar chart, one panel for alkalinity and one for sulfate, bars colored by feature type (well, well resort, spring, seep).",
  id = "fig-springswells"
)
```

```{r tbl-gainloss}
gl_tbl <- read.csv("data/derived/phreeqc/species_gainloss_summary_table.csv")
knitr::kable(
  gl_tbl, digits = 1, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Target", "Feature type", "Na", "SO4", "Si", "B", "K", "Alkalinity"),
  caption = "Real percent gain (+) or loss (-) relative to conservative mixing, by species and target, numeric companion to the heatmap above."
)
```

**How does the real temperature record fit into this, and is this a
chemically feasible connection for every feature type, or not?** The
three-stage cooling picture in @fig-tempprofile (Na/K reservoir estimate,
quartz-equilibration estimate, measured discharge temperature) and the
Steamboat Creek re-warming between SBRR and SBBV are both drawn directly
from values already reported above, placed side by side here as the
clearest single summary figure for this subsection. Put all of this
together and the honest answer is neither a clean "yes, connected" nor a
clean "no, not connected": the real Na/K reservoir-temperature agreement
(173-190 degrees Celsius across every real thermal feature, not just the
three used for the formal agreement test above) is consistent with one
shared deep source feeding wells, springs, and the seep alike. But the
sulfate, alkalinity, and quartz-versus-measured-temperature patterns above
show that **springs and wells diverge systematically in near-surface
process**, not randomly: springs and the seep show more cooling below their
own quartz-equilibration temperature and a consistent sulfate-gain/
alkalinity-loss signature that the wells do not share. The more precise and
more defensible statement, given this real baseline snapshot, is that these
features are chemically consistent with a shared deep source but **not**
chemically consistent with identical near-surface pathways: a specific,
testable distinction between spring-type and well-type connectivity that a
simple proximity map alone (SBS_0001 and SBW_0001 sit only 109 meters apart
yet show two of the most different fit behaviors on this flowpath, already
noted above) cannot provide on its own.

```{r fig-tempprofile}
  alt = "Two-panel figure: a line plot of temperature across three cooling stages for six features colored by type, and a two-point line plot showing creek temperature rising downstream.",
  id = "fig-tempprofile"
)
```

discharging among bedrock boulders at a location that had not been active
before, at a spot the two of us walk regularly; a nearby resident
separately confirmed this was new. We returned the following month to
photograph and GPS-log it (@fig-hotspring, all photos from September 27,
2026, within about 150 meters of each other at the terrace, times and
coordinates taken from camera EXIF data rather than our own notes). At the
same time we noted two other changes: a native-sulfur deposit
(@fig-sulfur) that has visibly grown and still looks fresh rather than
weathered, and a seep (@fig-seep) discharging from the alluvial cover
directly onto the underlying hard sinter bedrock, a concrete example of the
alluvium-to-bedrock contact the spring and well remapping below is designed
to document systematically rather than just stumbling across. Taken
together, these three observations support the poster's own conclusion
(fluids are still redistributing within an existing shallow conduit system
rather than the terrace having settled into a new, static state) and they
are the direct reason the remapping and monitoring work proposed below
needs to happen now rather than later.
